items.name: Loss Development
items.description: Loss development patterns must be measured and maintained for each line of business using paid and incurred triangles, with selected patterns reviewed at each analysis cycle. Material shifts in claim settlement or case reserving practice that distort development must be identified and adjusted for before patterns feed pricing or reserving work.

items.name: Loss Ratio Benchmarking
items.description: Loss ratios by line, segment, and program are compared against internal targets, plan assumptions, and available industry benchmarks on a regular cadence. Persistent deviations trigger root-cause analysis and a documented recommendation to pricing or underwriting leadership.

items.name: Territory and Class Analysis
items.description: Loss experience is segmented by territory and class of business to surface pockets of adverse or favorable performance hidden in aggregate results. Findings inform rate relativities, underwriting appetite, and growth strategy, with credibility procedures applied to thin segments.

items.name: Trend Analysis
items.description: Frequency and severity trends are quantified separately where data permits, drawing on internal experience, industry sources, and economic indicators such as medical and social inflation. Selected trend rates carry documented rationale and are revisited whenever observed experience diverges from prior selections.

items.name: Aggregate Tracking
items.description: Total insured values and modeled exposures are tracked continuously by peril, geography, and line of business as new and renewal business binds. The aggregation data must reconcile to policy administration systems and be refreshed frequently enough to support real-time underwriting referrals.

items.name: Annual Model Comparison
items.description: Each year the department compares output across the approved vendor models, and against prior-year results on a constant portfolio, to isolate the drivers of change. Material divergences between models or between versions are explained and reflected in the documented blending decision.

items.name: Approved Vendor Models
items.description: Only catastrophe models from vendors formally approved through the department's evaluation process may be used for pricing, accumulation, or capital purposes. The approved list specifies the perils, regions, and use cases each model is sanctioned for, and any use outside that scope requires documented exception approval.

items.name: Backtesting Against Historical Events
items.description: Modeled losses are reconciled against the carrier's actual experience from historical catastrophe events, including hurricanes, severe convective storms, and other relevant perils. Systematic over- or under-prediction is quantified and feeds adjustments to the carrier's own view of risk.

items.name: Concentration Limits
items.description: Board-approved concentration limits are maintained for each peril region, and exposure positions are measured against them on a defined cadence. Breaches or near-breaches trigger escalation to the chief actuary and chief underwriting officer with a documented remediation path.

items.name: Model Blending Approach Documented
items.description: Where multiple vendor models are blended to form the carrier's own view of risk, the blending weights, the rationale behind them, and any adjustments for non-modeled perils must be documented and approved. The blend is revisited when vendor releases or validation findings materially change relative model credibility.

items.name: PML Analysis
items.description: Probable maximum loss estimates are produced at the return periods relevant to reinsurance structuring, rating agency dialogue, and capital planning. Each PML run records the model version, portfolio snapshot date, and treatment of reinsurance so figures can be reproduced and compared over time.

items.name: Sensitivity Analysis
items.description: Model results are stress-tested for sensitivity to key inputs such as exposure data quality, secondary modifiers, demand surge, and event frequency assumptions. The analysis identifies which assumptions most influence the loss estimates so reviewers understand the uncertainty surrounding reported PMLs.

items.name: Version Control
items.description: The model version in production use is recorded for every analysis, and migrations to new vendor releases follow a controlled adoption process that quantifies the change in modeled losses before cutover. Results produced on superseded versions remain traceable to the version that generated them.

items.name: Zonal Reporting
items.description: Exposure is reported by defined catastrophe zones, including coastal tiers, earthquake zones, and wildfire-prone territories, in a format consumable by underwriting, reinsurance, and executive audiences. Zonal reports highlight period-over-period movement and flag zones approaching their limits.

items.name: Change Control
items.description: All modifications to the capital model follow a formal change process with documented justification, testing of the impact on results, and sign-off by the model owner before deployment. Emergency changes are permitted only with retrospective review and ratification.

items.name: Correlation Assumptions
items.description: Dependencies between risk types, lines of business, and entities are captured through documented correlation or copula assumptions with stated rationale and supporting evidence. Assumptions receive heightened scrutiny in the tail, where historical correlations tend to strengthen, and are reviewed on a regular cycle.

items.name: Diversification Benefit
items.description: The capital reduction attributed to diversification across the multi-line book is quantified, attributed back to its sources, and disclosed alongside undiversified figures. The benefit is tested for stability under stressed dependency assumptions before being relied upon in capital decisions.

items.name: Independent Validation
items.description: The model is validated on a defined cycle by reviewers independent of its development and operation, covering conceptual soundness, implementation accuracy, and outcome analysis. Validation findings are tracked to remediation and reported to the model governance committee.

items.name: Internal Capital Targets
items.description: Internal capital targets are set above regulatory minimums to reflect rating agency expectations, risk appetite, and growth plans, and are approved by the board. Actual capital positions are monitored against these targets with defined escalation thresholds well before regulatory action levels.

items.name: Model Documentation
items.description: The capital model's methodology, assumptions, data inputs, and known limitations are documented to a standard that allows a qualified actuary unfamiliar with the model to understand and rerun it. Documentation is kept current with each material model change.

items.name: Regulatory Capital Calculations
items.description: Risk-based capital and any other applicable regulatory capital measures are calculated accurately and on the prescribed schedule for each legal entity. Calculations reconcile to filed statutory statements, and movements between periods are explained to management before filing.

items.name: Risk Distribution by Source
items.description: Aggregate required capital is decomposed by risk source, including underwriting, reserve, catastrophe, market, credit, and operational risk, so management can see what drives the capital position. The attribution supports capital allocation to business units and pricing for the cost of capital.

items.name: Stress Testing
items.description: Capital adequacy is tested under a documented suite of adverse scenarios, including severe catastrophe seasons, reserve deterioration, investment shocks, and combined events. Stress results inform contingency capital plans and are presented to the risk committee at least annually.

items.name: Version Control
items.description: Every production run of the capital model is tied to a specific, archived model version, with code, parameters, and input data preserved. Superseded versions remain retrievable so historical capital figures can be reproduced for auditors and regulators.

items.name: Actual Versus Expected Analysis
items.description: Emerging loss, frequency, and severity experience is compared against the assumptions embedded in current rates on a regular cadence by line and segment. Deviations are decomposed into their drivers, distinguishing random volatility from genuine assumption misses.

items.name: Actuarial Indication Basis
items.description: Rate indications are produced on a consistent, documented basis specifying the experience period, premium on-level adjustments, loss trending, and credibility procedures. Departures of filed or implemented rates from the actuarial indication are recorded with business rationale.

items.name: Actuarial Memorandum
items.description: Each rate filing includes an actuarial memorandum prepared in accordance with applicable Actuarial Standards of Practice, describing the data, methods, assumptions, and judgments behind the requested rate change. The memorandum is signed by a qualified actuary who takes responsibility for the work.

items.name: Adjustment Recommendations
items.description: When monitored experience diverges materially from expectations, the department issues documented recommendations covering rate level, segmentation, or underwriting action, with quantified support. Recommendations are tracked through to disposition so accepted and rejected actions are both on record.

items.name: Annual Rate Adequacy Analysis
items.description: Every rated line of business undergoes a formal rate adequacy study at least annually, comparing current rate levels to indicated levels. Lines found inadequate carry a documented action plan, whether a filing, underwriting tightening, or accepted deviation with rationale.

items.name: Documented Pricing Approach by Line of Business
items.description: Each line of business maintains a written pricing methodology covering data sources, ratemaking technique, expense and profit provisions, and treatment of reinsurance costs. The documentation is owned by a named actuary and updated whenever the approach materially changes.

items.name: Loss Development Factors
items.description: Development factors used in ratemaking are derived from current triangles using documented selection criteria, with consistency checks against the factors used in reserving. Selections are refreshed each pricing cycle and material changes from prior selections are explained.

items.name: Loss Ratio Projections
items.description: Prospective loss ratios are projected for the period the rates will be in effect, reflecting trended losses, on-level premium, and expected mix shifts. Projections state their key assumptions and are reconciled retrospectively against actual results to sharpen future analyses.

items.name: Pricing Feedback Loop
items.description: Monitoring findings flow back into the next pricing review through a defined process connecting the monitoring team, pricing actuaries, and underwriting. The loop ensures assumption updates are grounded in observed experience rather than carried forward by inertia.

items.name: Regulatory Response Coordination
items.description: Objections and interrogatories from state insurance departments are routed through a defined process pairing the filing actuary with compliance, with response deadlines tracked and met. Responses are reviewed for technical accuracy and consistency with positions taken in other jurisdictions.

items.name: Supporting Exhibits
items.description: Filings are accompanied by exhibits presenting the experience data, development, trend, on-level calculations, and indicated versus selected rates in the format each state expects. Exhibits must tie to the underlying analysis workpapers without manual reconciliation gaps.

items.name: Trend Assumptions Documented
items.description: The frequency, severity, and premium trend assumptions underlying each adequacy review are recorded with their data sources and selection rationale. Reviewers can therefore trace any indicated rate need back to the specific trend selections that produced it.

items.name: Actuarial Certification
items.description: Where states require certification that filed rates are not excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory, a qualified actuary performs the supporting review and signs the certification. The certifying actuary's workpapers are retained as evidence of the basis for the opinion.

items.name: Competitive Analysis
items.description: Proposed rates are benchmarked against competitor filings and market intelligence to assess positioning by segment and the risk of adverse selection. The analysis distinguishes deliberate competitive stances from unintended pricing gaps before launch approval.

items.name: New Product Actuarial Sign-Off
items.description: No new product launches without documented sign-off from the responsible pricing actuary covering the rating plan, assumptions, and expected profitability. The sign-off identifies key uncertainties and the monitoring plan that will validate assumptions post-launch.

items.name: Objection Response
items.description: Actuarial objections raised against product filings are answered with technically complete responses within regulator deadlines, coordinated with product and compliance teams. Recurring objection themes are catalogued and fed back into filing preparation to reduce future cycle time.

items.name: Profit Testing
items.description: New products are profit-tested against the carrier's return targets using projected loss ratios, expenses, persistency, and cost of capital, with sensitivity runs on the most uncertain assumptions. Products failing the hurdle require redesign or explicit executive acceptance of the shortfall.

items.name: Rate and Form Filing Support
items.description: Actuarial staff supply the rate exhibits, rating algorithm specifications, and actuarial justification needed for rate and form filings across the product portfolio. Support includes verifying that filed rating rules can actually be implemented as described in policy administration systems.

items.name: Ceded Pricing Analysis
items.description: Quoted reinsurance terms are evaluated against the department's own loss cost estimates for the ceded layers, derived from experience and exposure rating. The analysis expresses each quote as a rate-on-line and expected economic margin so negotiators understand what they are paying for risk transfer.

items.name: Ceded Reserve Calculation
items.description: Ceded loss and loss adjustment expense reserves are calculated by treaty in accordance with contract terms, including attachment points, limits, and reinstatement provisions. Ceded figures reconcile to gross and net reserve analyses so the three views remain internally consistent.

items.name: Collectability Analysis
items.description: Recoverables are assessed for collectability based on reinsurer financial strength, ratings, disputes, and aging of paid balances, with provisions for uncollectible amounts established where warranted. Concentrations with individual reinsurers are monitored against counterparty limits.

items.name: Commutation Support
items.description: When treaty commutations are contemplated, the department values the ceded liabilities being extinguished, including discounting and risk margins, to support negotiation of the commutation price. The analysis quantifies the balance sheet and income impact of accepting versus declining the commutation.

items.name: Retrocession Analysis Support
items.description: Where the carrier assumes business or participates in structures with retrocession features, the department analyzes the retro protections available and their effect on net positions. Support covers pricing the retro layers and assessing counterparty and basis risk in the proposed cover.

items.name: Treaty Optimization
items.description: Alternative program structures, including retention levels, layer boundaries, and quota share versus excess arrangements, are modeled for their effect on net volatility, capital relief, and expected cost. Recommendations to the reinsurance buying team balance earnings protection against ceded margin.

items.name: Board Reporting
items.description: The chief actuary delivers periodic reporting to the board and its committees covering reserve adequacy, pricing trends, catastrophe exposure, and emerging risks, in language suited to a governance audience. Material adverse developments are escalated between scheduled cycles rather than held for the next meeting.

items.name: Management Dashboards
items.description: Operational dashboards present key actuarial indicators, including loss ratio trends, reserve movements, and rate change achievement, refreshed on a defined schedule. Metrics carry consistent definitions across business units so management comparisons are like-for-like.

items.name: ORSA Support
items.description: The department supplies the quantitative content for the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment, including capital projections, stress scenarios, and risk quantification across the planning horizon. Contributions align with the capital model and risk appetite framework so the ORSA tells one consistent story.

items.name: Regulatory Statements
items.description: Actuarial inputs to statutory filings, including Schedule P support and the Statement of Actuarial Opinion, are produced accurately and on the regulatory calendar. Figures in regulatory statements reconcile to internal analyses, with differences in basis documented.

items.name: Actuarial Report with Key Assumptions
items.description: Each reserve review produces a formal actuarial report meeting ASOP 41 communication standards, setting out data, methods, key assumptions, and the basis for selections. The report is sufficient for another qualified actuary to assess the reasonableness of the conclusions.

items.name: Development Factor Derivation
items.description: Age-to-age factors are derived using stated averaging conventions, with outlier treatment, tail factor methodology, and the rationale for final selections recorded. Selected factors are compared against prior selections and industry benchmarks to confirm reasonableness.

items.name: IBNR Factors by Line of Business and Accident Year
items.description: IBNR is estimated at the level of line of business and accident year, using factors derived from the selected development patterns and expected loss methods appropriate to each cohort's maturity. Factor selections are documented and reconciled to the prior review so movements are explainable.

items.name: Management Summary
items.description: A concise summary translates the technical findings into the booked reserve recommendation, the drivers of change, and the principal uncertainties, written for senior management and the audit committee. The summary states clearly where the recommendation sits relative to the actuarial central estimate.

items.name: Methods Documented by Line of Business
items.description: The reserving methods applied to each line, such as chain ladder, Bornhuetter-Ferguson, and expected loss ratio approaches, are documented along with the criteria for weighting them by accident year maturity. Method changes require justification and quantification of their impact before adoption.

items.name: Monthly Reserve Review
items.description: Actual loss emergence is compared to expected each month at a summary level, with material deviations investigated and escalated to the chief actuary. The monthly process is designed to surface deterioration quickly rather than re-estimate the full reserve.

items.name: Quarterly Deep Dive
items.description: A full reserve study updating triangles, selections, and IBNR is performed each quarter, with results presented to management before the financial close. Each quarter rotates additional focus onto lines showing volatility or strategic significance.

items.name: Range of Estimates
items.description: A reasonable range around the central IBNR estimate is produced and communicated, with the booked position located explicitly within that range. Movement of the booked reserve relative to the range over time is monitored as an indicator of reserving strength or weakening.

items.name: Sensitivity Analysis
items.description: The IBNR estimate is tested for sensitivity to the key assumptions, including tail factors, trend, and expected loss ratios, quantifying how plausible alternative selections would move the booked reserve. Results inform management's understanding of where the estimate is most fragile.

items.name: Triangle Selection
items.description: The choice of triangle basis for each analysis, including paid versus incurred, accident versus report year, and the level of segmentation, is documented with rationale tied to the line's claim characteristics. Segmentation is revisited when business mix or volume changes erode the homogeneity or credibility of existing groupings.

items.name: Variance Explanation
items.description: Differences between the current estimate and the prior review, and between actual emergence and what was expected, are quantified and attributed to their causes. Persistent one-directional variances are flagged as potential evidence of assumption bias requiring correction.

items.name: Year-End External Review
items.description: The year-end reserve position is subject to independent review by an external actuarial firm or appointed actuary engagement, supporting the Statement of Actuarial Opinion. Differences between external and internal estimates are reconciled and reported to the audit committee.

items.name: Actuarial Opinion Sign-Off
items.description: Formal opinions, including the Statement of Actuarial Opinion on reserves, are signed only by appointed actuaries meeting the qualification standards of the American Academy of Actuaries. The signing actuary maintains the supporting actuarial opinion summary and workpapers required by regulators.

items.name: Compliance with Actuarial Standards of Practice
items.description: All actuarial work products comply with the applicable ASOPs issued by the Actuarial Standards Board, including those governing data quality, assumptions, and communications. Deviations from a standard are permitted only where the ASOP itself allows and must be disclosed in the work product.

items.name: Data Validation
items.description: Data received for actuarial use is checked for reasonableness, completeness, and internal consistency before analysis begins, consistent with ASOP 23. Anomalies such as negative payments, missing accident dates, or implausible values are investigated and their treatment documented.

items.name: Known Data Limitations Documented
items.description: Limitations in the available data, such as system conversions, coding changes, or thin volume in newer segments, are catalogued and disclosed in the work products that rely on the data. Analysts document how each limitation was addressed and its potential effect on the conclusions.

items.name: Peer Review Process
items.description: Significant analyses, including reserve studies, rate indications, and capital work, receive documented peer review by a qualified actuary not involved in the original work before release. Review comments and their resolution are retained with the workpapers.

items.name: Reconciliation to Source Systems
items.description: Actuarial data extracts are reconciled to the policy, claims, and general ledger systems they originate from, with premium and loss totals tied out each analysis cycle. Unreconciled differences beyond defined tolerances must be resolved or explained before the data is used.

items.name: Assigned to Adjuster Within 24 Hours
items.description: New claims must be triaged for line of business, severity, and complexity and assigned to an appropriately licensed and authorized adjuster within 24 hours of FNOL receipt. Assignments that cannot be completed in that window, such as catastrophe surge volumes, require supervisor notation explaining the delay and the interim handling plan.

items.name: Contact Attempts Documented
items.description: Every attempt to reach the insured, whether successful or not, must be recorded in the claim system with the date, time, channel used, and outcome. This record demonstrates good-faith handling in the event of a regulatory inquiry or bad-faith allegation and allows supervisors to verify the contact standard was met.

items.name: Coverage Confirmed Within 24 Hours of Assignment
items.description: Upon assignment, the adjuster must review the policy in force, applicable endorsements, and loss facts to confirm whether coverage applies, completing the determination within 24 hours. Where coverage cannot yet be confirmed, the file must document the open questions and any reservation of rights consideration before the deadline passes.

items.name: Denial Letters Within 72 Hours if No Coverage
items.description: When the coverage review concludes that no coverage exists, a written denial letter citing the specific policy provisions relied upon must be issued to the insured within 72 hours. The letter must follow approved template language, reference state-specific notice requirements, and be retained in the claim file alongside the supporting coverage analysis.

items.name: FNOL Acknowledged Within 4 Hours
items.description: Each first notice of loss, regardless of intake channel, must be acknowledged to the reporting party within 4 hours of receipt with a claim number and a description of what happens next. The acknowledgment timestamp is captured in the claim system and monitored against the SLA on intake dashboards.

items.name: Insured Contacted Within 24 Hours of Assignment
items.description: The assigned adjuster must make first contact with the insured within 24 hours of receiving the file, explaining the claims process, confirming loss details, and setting expectations for next steps. Contact by phone is preferred, with email or letter acceptable only after live contact attempts have failed.

items.name: Documented Red Flag Checklist
items.description: Adjusters must apply a standardized red flag checklist covering indicators such as late reporting, prior claim history, inconsistent statements, and financial distress, and record the results in the claim file. The checklist is maintained by SIU, reviewed annually against emerging fraud schemes, and completion is a required step before significant payments are released.

items.name: Investigation Plan Within 5 Days
items.description: Within 5 days of accepting a referral, the SIU investigator must produce a written investigation plan identifying the suspected scheme, evidence to be gathered, interviews to be conducted, and target milestones. The plan is approved by the SIU manager and updated as the investigation develops.

items.name: Law Enforcement Coordination Documented
items.description: Any contact with law enforcement, state fraud bureaus, or the National Insurance Crime Bureau must be recorded in the SIU case file, including the agency, contact person, information shared, and statutory immunity provisions relied upon. Mandatory fraud reporting obligations in each jurisdiction must be satisfied and evidenced in the file.

items.name: Outcome Tracked
items.description: Each SIU case must be closed with a recorded disposition, such as fraud substantiated, unsubstantiated, claim withdrawn, or referred for prosecution, along with any savings or restitution attributed to the investigation. Aggregated outcomes feed SIU performance reporting and annual fraud plan filings where states require them.

items.name: Referral to SIU Within 48 Hours if Triggered
items.description: When checklist results or adjuster judgment indicate potential fraud, the claim must be referred to the Special Investigation Unit within 48 hours of the trigger being identified. The referral must summarize the indicators observed, and routine claim activity that could prejudice the investigation is paused pending SIU direction.

items.name: All Claim Activity Documented in System Within 24 Hours
items.description: Calls, inspections, coverage analyses, reserve rationale, and all other material claim activity must be entered into the claim system within 24 hours of occurring. Notes must be factual and professional, as the file may be produced in litigation or regulatory examination.

items.name: Expert Engagement
items.description: Independent adjusters, engineers, appraisers, and other outside experts may be retained only in accordance with the department's authority matrix, which defines who may approve the engagement, the approved vendor panels to draw from, and the expense thresholds requiring escalation. This keeps expert spend controlled and ensures specialists are used where claim complexity genuinely warrants them.

items.name: Photos and Evidence Linked to File
items.description: Photographs, estimates, police reports, recorded statements, and other evidentiary materials must be uploaded and attached to the correct claim file rather than held in email or local storage. Each item should be labeled with its source and date so the evidentiary chain remains intact through settlement, subrogation, or litigation.

items.name: Recorded Statements Within 14 Days
items.description: Recorded statements from the insured, claimants, and material witnesses must be obtained within 14 days of assignment where a statement is warranted by the loss type or liability questions. Statements must follow approved question outlines, include the required consent language, and be transcribed or summarized into the claim file.

items.name: Scene Inspection Within 72 Hours for Property
items.description: For property losses, the damaged premises or scene must be inspected within 72 hours of assignment, either by the handling adjuster or an approved field resource. Prompt inspection preserves perishable evidence, supports accurate scoping of damages, and reduces the risk of disputes over pre-existing conditions.

items.name: Subrogation Potential Identified
items.description: During the initial investigation the adjuster must assess whether a third party may be legally responsible for the loss and flag the file for subrogation review when potential exists. Evidence supporting recovery, such as defective products or at-fault driver information, must be preserved and the statute of limitations noted.

items.name: Defense Counsel From Approved Panel
items.description: Defense of litigated claims must be assigned to firms on the carrier's approved panel, which is vetted for jurisdiction expertise, rate agreements, and adherence to billing and reporting guidelines. Use of non-panel counsel requires advance approval from the litigation manager with documented justification, such as a conflict or a specialty not represented on the panel.

items.name: Litigation Plan Required
items.description: Within the period set by counsel guidelines, defense counsel must submit a litigation plan covering liability assessment, damages evaluation, discovery strategy, motion practice, resolution strategy, and budget. The claims professional reviews and approves the plan and holds counsel to it at defined case milestones.

items.name: Reserve Adjusted for Legal Exposure
items.description: Once suit is filed or litigation becomes probable, the reserve must be reevaluated to reflect verdict potential, defense costs, and jurisdiction-specific factors rather than the pre-suit damages estimate alone. Reserve changes driven by litigation developments must be documented with counsel's evaluation as support.

items.name: 10% of Files Reviewed Monthly
items.description: Each month a sample equal to at least 10 percent of open and recently closed files per adjuster is selected for quality review against the department's audit criteria. Sampling must include a mix of claim types and severities, with targeted pulls added when prior reviews identified deficiencies.

items.name: Auto: 30 Days Average
items.description: Auto physical damage and routine auto claims should resolve in an average of 30 days from FNOL to closure. Files open beyond the benchmark are flagged on aging reports for supervisor review of what is blocking resolution, such as parts delays or unresponsive parties.

items.name: Calibration Sessions Quarterly
items.description: Quality reviewers and claims managers meet each quarter to score a common set of files and reconcile differences in interpretation of the audit criteria. Calibration outcomes are documented and the audit guide updated where the sessions reveal ambiguous standards.

items.name: Complaints Escalated Within 24 Hours
items.description: Customer complaints received through any channel, including department of insurance inquiries, must be escalated to the designated complaint handler within 24 hours of receipt. Each complaint is logged, investigated, and answered within regulatory timeframes, with outcomes fed back into quality reviews.

items.name: Complex: 180 Days Average
items.description: Claims designated complex, such as large losses, coverage disputes, or serious injury cases, are managed to a 180-day average. The extended target recognizes legitimate investigative and legal timelines while still requiring quarterly file strategy reviews to keep the claim progressing.

items.name: Liability: 90 Days Average
items.description: Liability claims are targeted to close within an average of 90 days, allowing for liability investigation, injury evaluation, and negotiation while discouraging files from drifting without active handling. Claims exceeding the average require a documented action plan toward resolution.

items.name: NPS Target Above 40
items.description: The department maintains a Net Promoter Score target of greater than 40 across closed-claim surveys, monitored monthly by line of business. Scores trending below target trigger root-cause review of detractor feedback and corrective action plans owned by claims leadership.

items.name: Post-Claim Survey Sent
items.description: A satisfaction survey must be issued to the insured after claim closure through the standard survey platform, covering responsiveness, communication clarity, and fairness of outcome. Response data is attributed to the handling adjuster and office for coaching and trend analysis.

items.name: Property: 45 Days Average
items.description: Property claims carry a 45-day average cycle time target, reflecting the additional time needed for inspection, scoping, and contractor estimates. Catastrophe-coded losses are measured separately so surge events do not distort the standard book's performance.

items.name: Quality Scorecard Maintained
items.description: Review results are recorded on a standardized scorecard measuring dimensions such as coverage analysis, contact compliance, reserve accuracy, and documentation quality. Scores roll up to adjuster, team, and office levels and inform coaching plans, training priorities, and performance evaluations.

items.name: Facultative Claims Reported Within 72 Hours
items.description: Losses on policies with facultative reinsurance must be reported to the facultative reinsurer within 72 hours of the claim being identified as touching the certificate. Because facultative placements are policy-specific and often contain strict claims-cooperation clauses, late notice risks the recoverable, so the 72-hour internal standard deliberately runs ahead of most certificate requirements.

items.name: Treaty Notification Per Contract Terms
items.description: Claims that meet or are likely to meet treaty attachment points, or that fall within categories the treaty designates as reportable regardless of size, must be noticed to the reinsurer within the timeframes and in the format the treaty specifies. The claims team coordinates with the ceded reinsurance function to confirm reporting thresholds for each program year and documents the notification in the claim file.

items.name: Claims Over $100K Require Senior Adjuster Assignment
items.description: Any claim with incurred value or realistic exposure exceeding $100,000 must be assigned or reassigned to a senior adjuster with the experience and authority appropriate to large losses. The reassignment is made promptly once the threshold is recognized, with a documented file transfer summarizing status and open actions.

items.name: Documented Rationale Required
items.description: The basis for the initial reserve, including damages assumptions, liability assessment, and any comparable claim references, must be recorded in the claim file alongside the worksheet. This rationale gives subsequent reserve reviews a baseline and supports actuarial and audit reliance on case reserve data.

items.name: Initial Reserve Set Within 72 Hours Based on Reserve Worksheet
items.description: The handling adjuster must establish an initial case reserve within 72 hours of assignment using the standard reserve worksheet, which walks through indemnity components, expected expenses, and applicable deductibles or limits. Placeholder or formula-only reserves are acceptable solely as a system default pending the worksheet-based evaluation.

items.name: Manager Approval for Changes Over $25K
items.description: Any single reserve change exceeding $25,000, upward or downward, requires manager review and approval before posting. The approval captures the development driving the change and guards against both stair-stepped under-reserving and unexplained reserve takedowns.

items.name: Over $500K Requires Manager Oversight
items.description: Claims exceeding $500,000 in incurred value or exposure are placed under active manager oversight, including participation in reserve and settlement decisions and periodic strategy reviews documented in the file. These claims also feed the large loss report distributed to claims leadership, actuarial, and ceded reinsurance.

items.name: Reserves Reviewed at 30, 60, and 90 Days
items.description: Open claims must undergo a documented reserve adequacy review at the 30, 60, and 90 day marks, with the adjuster confirming the reserve still reflects known damages, liability posture, and expense expectations. Each review note must either affirm the current reserve with reasoning or record the adjustment made.

items.name: Adjuster Authority Per Level
items.description: Each adjuster holds documented settlement authority tied to their grade, license status, and demonstrated performance, and may not commit the carrier beyond that limit. Settlements above an individual's authority must be escalated for approval before any offer is extended, and authority grants are reviewed annually.

items.name: Manager Approval for Policy Limits Settlements
items.description: Any settlement at or near policy limits requires manager approval before the offer is made or accepted, given the bad-faith exposure attached to limits demands. The approval must be documented with the manager's evaluation of liability, damages, and the timing of the demand.

items.name: No Nuisance Payments
items.description: Claims without supporting liability or damages may not be settled simply to avoid handling or defense costs. Every payment must be justified by the documented merits of the claim, preserving the integrity of loss data and avoiding signaling that meritless claims will be paid.

items.name: Payments Issued Within 5 Business Days of Settlement Agreement
items.description: Once a settlement is agreed and all payment conditions are satisfied, the indemnity payment must be issued within 5 business days. Prompt payment supports state prompt-pay statutes and customer satisfaction commitments, and aging of approved-but-unpaid settlements is monitored on operations reports.

items.name: Proper Payee Verification
items.description: Before release, the adjuster must verify the payee's identity and entitlement, including correct legal names, lienholder and mortgagee interests, attorney representation, and any required multi-party endorsements. Bank detail changes or unusual payment instructions must be independently confirmed to guard against payment redirection fraud.

items.name: Signed Release Required Before Payment
items.description: Settlement payments to claimants may not be issued until a release appropriate to the claim type and jurisdiction has been signed and returned. The release must use approved template language, identify all released parties and claims, and be reviewed for alterations before payment is authorized.

items.name: Subrogation Rights Preserved Where Applicable
items.description: Release and settlement documents must be drafted so they do not extinguish the carrier's subrogation or contribution rights against responsible third parties. Where recovery potential exists, the file must confirm that the executed release language protects those rights before the claim is closed.

items.name: Contingency Fee Approval
items.description: Engaging outside recovery vendors or counsel on a contingency fee basis requires advance approval at the designated authority level, with the fee percentage and case-selection criteria documented. Approved arrangements are monitored for net recovery performance to confirm contingency placement outperforms in-house pursuit for the referred inventory.

items.name: Recovery Tracked to Closure
items.description: Each referred subrogation matter must be tracked from demand through negotiation, arbitration, or litigation until funds are collected or the pursuit is formally closed with a documented reason. Recoveries are recorded against the originating claim so net loss figures and deductible reimbursements to insureds are accurate.

items.name: Subrogation Potential Evaluated on Every Claim
items.description: A subrogation assessment is a mandatory step on every claim, with the adjuster recording whether recovery potential exists and the basis for that conclusion. Files with potential are referred to the subrogation unit with the supporting evidence preserved, and a no-potential determination must be affirmatively documented rather than left blank.

items.name: Annual Compliance Training
items.description: All employees and contingent workers complete a core compliance curriculum at least once per year covering topics such as privacy, anti-fraud, unfair trade practices, and reporting obligations. New hires receive the training within a defined onboarding window before assuming regulated duties.

items.name: Annual Effectiveness Review
items.description: An evaluation of the compliance program's design and operating effectiveness is performed at least annually, assessing coverage of regulatory obligations, adequacy of staffing and tooling, and outcomes of testing and issue remediation. Results and recommended enhancements are reported to senior management and the Board.

items.name: Board Oversight
items.description: The Board of Directors, or a designated committee, exercises documented oversight of the compliance program, including approving the program charter and receiving regular reports on compliance posture, significant matters, and resource adequacy. Minutes must evidence the Board's review and any direction given to management.

items.name: Completion Tracking
items.description: Training assignments, completions, and assessment results are recorded in the learning management system, with automated reminders for approaching deadlines and escalation to managers for past-due items. Completion rates are reported to compliance leadership and retained as evidence for regulatory examinations.

items.name: Findings Tracked
items.description: Every testing exception is logged in the compliance issue register with a severity rating, accountable owner, remediation plan, and due date. Open findings are monitored to closure, with aging and overdue items escalated to compliance leadership and reflected in management reporting.

items.name: Risk-Based Testing Plan
items.description: Compliance testing coverage is determined by a documented risk assessment that weighs regulatory exposure, prior findings, business volume, and recent change in each area, with higher-risk processes such as claims handling and producer licensing tested more frequently and in greater depth. The plan and its risk rationale are approved by the Chief Compliance Officer annually.

items.name: Role-Specific Modules
items.description: Supplemental training is assigned based on job function, so that claims adjusters, underwriters, producers, and customer-facing staff receive instruction on the regulations and conduct standards specific to their roles, such as fair claims settlement practices or suitability rules for annuity sales. Module assignments are reviewed when an employee changes roles.

items.name: Testing Calendar
items.description: A forward-looking calendar schedules each test engagement across the year, identifying the business area, scope, assigned tester, and target completion date. The calendar is maintained centrally, and deferrals or scope changes require documented approval so coverage commitments remain visible.

items.name: Written Compliance Program
items.description: A formal, documented compliance program must be maintained that defines the program's scope, governance structure, key compliance obligations across P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits lines, and the roles responsible for execution. The document is approved by the Chief Compliance Officer and updated whenever material regulatory or organizational changes occur.

items.name: Action Plans Tracked
items.description: Where residual risk exceeds tolerance, remediation action plans are recorded with defined milestones, target dates, and required resources, and progress is tracked through the ERM system. Slipping or stalled plans are escalated through risk committee reporting until completed or formally re-scoped.

items.name: Annual Risk Assessment
items.description: A structured enterprise-wide risk identification exercise is conducted at least annually, engaging business unit leaders, risk owners, and subject matter experts across P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits operations to surface new and changed risks. Results feed the risk inventory and the assessment and reporting processes.

items.name: Board-Approved Risk Appetite
items.description: The enterprise risk appetite statement must be formally approved by the Board of Directors, articulating the types and aggregate level of risk the carrier will accept in pursuit of its strategy across underwriting, market, credit, operational, and reputational dimensions. Material amendments require re-approval rather than management-level revision.

items.name: Control Activities Documented
items.description: Controls that mitigate each material risk are formally documented, describing the control objective, how the control operates, its frequency, and the evidence it produces. Documentation is kept current so control effectiveness can be assessed and relied upon in residual risk ratings.

items.name: Emerging Risks Monitored
items.description: A defined process scans for emerging risks such as climate-driven loss trends, AI and model risk, cyber threats, and shifting regulatory expectations, drawing on industry sources, regulator publications, and internal indicators. Candidate emerging risks are evaluated for relevance and, where warranted, formally added to the inventory with an assigned owner.

items.name: Escalation Triggers Defined
items.description: Objective thresholds specify when a risk event, limit breach, or indicator deterioration must be escalated outside the normal reporting cycle, including to whom and within what timeframe. Triggers are documented in the ERM framework and tested periodically so escalation operates reliably under stress.

items.name: Heat Maps Maintained
items.description: Assessment results are maintained in heat map form plotting likelihood against impact for the enterprise and for each major business segment, refreshed on the established assessment cycle. Heat maps accompany risk reporting so leadership and the Board can see concentration and movement of top risks at a glance.

items.name: Inherent and Residual Risk
items.description: Risks are assessed both on an inherent basis, before considering controls, and on a residual basis after evaluating control design and effectiveness, making the value of the control environment explicit. Residual ratings that exceed appetite trigger documented treatment decisions.

items.name: Likelihood and Impact Scoring
items.description: Each risk in the enterprise inventory is scored on standardized likelihood and impact scales with defined rating criteria, including financial, regulatory, operational, and reputational impact dimensions. Scoring definitions are calibrated so ratings are comparable across business units and risk categories.

items.name: Monthly Risk Dashboard
items.description: A risk dashboard is produced each month for senior management summarizing key risk indicators, limit utilization against appetite, top and emerging risks, and the status of significant mitigation plans. Metrics are sourced from the risk inventory and operational systems so the dashboard reflects current data rather than narrative alone.

items.name: Quantitative and Qualitative Limits
items.description: The appetite statement is operationalized through measurable limits, such as capital-at-risk thresholds, catastrophe exposure ceilings, and counterparty concentration caps, alongside qualitative expressions for risks that resist quantification, such as conduct and reputational risk. Tolerances and limit breaches are defined so monitoring against appetite is objective.

items.name: Quarterly Board Report
items.description: The Chief Risk Officer delivers a quarterly report to the Board or its risk committee covering the enterprise risk profile relative to appetite, material changes since the prior quarter, stress and scenario results where applicable, and matters requiring Board attention. The report and the Board's discussion are documented in committee records.

items.name: Reviewed Annually
items.description: The risk appetite statement is reviewed at least once per year against the current strategic plan, capital position, and external environment, with the review and any resulting changes documented and presented to the Board. Off-cycle reviews are triggered by significant events such as acquisitions or major shifts in market conditions.

items.name: Risk Inventory Maintained
items.description: A central inventory records every identified risk with its description, category, owner, current ratings, and linkage to controls and mitigation plans. The inventory is the authoritative source for risk reporting and is updated as risks are added, re-rated, or retired.

items.name: Risk Owners Accountable
items.description: Every material risk has a named owner at an appropriate level of seniority who is responsible for the accuracy of the risk's assessment, the adequacy of its controls, and the delivery of its action plans. Ownership assignments are reviewed when organizational changes occur so accountability never lapses.

items.name: Annual Acknowledgment
items.description: Each employee, officer, and director formally acknowledges the code of conduct every year, attesting that they have read it, understand it, and have disclosed any matters it requires. Acknowledgments are captured electronically with completion monitored and non-responders escalated to management.

items.name: Annual Disclosure
items.description: All employees, officers, and directors complete a conflicts of interest disclosure at least annually, declaring outside business activities, financial interests, family relationships with vendors or competitors, and any other circumstances that could impair objectivity. Material changes arising mid-year must be disclosed promptly rather than held for the next cycle.

items.name: Anonymous Reporting Channel
items.description: A reporting channel operated by an independent third party is available around the clock by phone and web, allowing employees, contractors, and producers to raise concerns anonymously in their preferred language. The channel's existence and access details are publicized through training, the intranet, and workplace postings.

items.name: Available in Multiple Languages
items.description: The code of conduct is published in the primary languages of the workforce so that comprehension is not limited by English proficiency, with translations maintained in step with each revision of the English master. Accessibility of all language versions is verified on the company intranet and in onboarding materials.

items.name: Investigation Protocol
items.description: Reported matters follow a documented protocol covering intake triage, severity classification, assignment to qualified investigators, evidence handling, confidentiality safeguards, and timeframes for resolution. Outcomes, substantiation rates, and significant matters are reported to the audit committee, and case records are retained per the retention schedule.

items.name: Mitigation Plans
items.description: Where a disclosed conflict cannot simply be eliminated, a written mitigation plan specifies the safeguards applied, such as transferring duties, restricting information access, or adding independent oversight to affected decisions. Plans are monitored for adherence and revisited when the underlying circumstances change.

items.name: Non-Retaliation Policy
items.description: A formal policy prohibits retaliation in any form against individuals who report concerns in good faith or participate in investigations, with violations treated as serious misconduct subject to discipline up to termination. Reporters who allege retaliation receive a separate, prioritized review.

items.name: Recusal Requirements
items.description: Individuals with a conflict must recuse themselves from decisions, approvals, and deliberations the conflict touches, including vendor selection, claims determinations, hiring, and investment actions. Recusals are documented in the relevant decision record so the integrity of the outcome can be demonstrated afterward.

items.name: Review Process
items.description: Submitted disclosures are reviewed by the compliance function against defined criteria, with potentially significant conflicts referred to the ethics committee or designated senior officer for determination. Review outcomes and their rationale are documented and retained.

items.name: Training Required
items.description: Training on the code of conduct is mandatory for all personnel, reinforcing key provisions such as fair treatment of policyholders, anti-bribery expectations, confidentiality, and the duty to report suspected misconduct. Content is refreshed periodically and incorporated into new-hire onboarding before access to sensitive systems or customer data is granted.

items.name: Complaint Tracking
items.description: All complaints, whether received directly, through producers, or via state insurance departments, are logged in a central system with the complainant, product line, issue category, and handling history. The log distinguishes department-of-insurance complaints from direct complaints, since each carries distinct regulatory handling obligations.

items.name: Disclosure Standards
items.description: Consumers must receive required disclosures at the prescribed points in the sales process, including buyer's guides, policy summaries, illustration certifications, and replacement notices where applicable, in clear language and approved formats. Sales materials and disclosures are subject to advertising review before use.

items.name: Documentation
items.description: Each claim file must contain a complete record of the investigation, correspondence, evaluation rationale, reserve changes, and settlement basis, sufficient for an independent reviewer or market conduct examiner to reconstruct how the outcome was reached. File documentation standards are enforced through supervisory review and periodic quality audits.

items.name: Regulatory Reporting
items.description: Complaint records are maintained in the form and detail required for state market conduct annual statement filings and examination requests, and required complaint registers are produced accurately and on time. Data quality checks ensure reported figures reconcile to the tracking system.

items.name: Response Timelines
items.description: Complaints are acknowledged and substantively answered within defined timeframes that meet or exceed each state's requirements, with department-of-insurance inquiries answered by their stated due dates without exception. Approaching deadlines generate automated alerts and unresolved cases are escalated to supervisors.

items.name: Root Cause Analysis
items.description: Complaint data is analyzed periodically to identify recurring causes, such as a confusing policy provision, a billing system defect, or a producer conduct pattern, and findings are routed to the owning business area for corrective action. Trends and remediation status are reported to compliance leadership.

items.name: Suitability Requirements
items.description: Recommendations of annuities, life insurance, and other covered products must be grounded in a documented assessment of the consumer's financial situation, objectives, and needs, consistent with the NAIC suitability and best interest standards adopted in each state. Suitability documentation is captured at point of sale and reviewed before the transaction is accepted.

items.name: Supervision Requirements
items.description: A supervisory system monitors producer sales activity through transaction review, replacement and lapse pattern analysis, and complaint signals, with defined escalation when red flags appear. Supervisory responsibilities, review evidence, and disciplinary outcomes are documented to demonstrate effective oversight of both captive and independent distribution.

items.name: Timing Requirements
items.description: Acknowledgment of claims, requests for information, coverage decisions, and payment issuance must each occur within the timeframes prescribed by applicable state regulations, applying the strictest standard where the company elects a uniform internal benchmark. Cycle times are monitored and aged claims are escalated before regulatory deadlines are breached.

items.name: Unfair Claims Practices Compliance
items.description: Claims operations must conform to the unfair claims settlement practices acts of every state in which the carrier writes business, including prohibitions on misrepresenting policy provisions, compelling litigation through lowball offers, and failing to act in good faith on claims where liability is clear. Procedures, adjuster guidance, and quality reviews are mapped to these statutory requirements.

items.name: Approval Authority
items.description: Exception requests are decided by the designated approval authority, which scales with the risk involved, ranging from the policy owner for low-risk deviations to the relevant executive or risk committee for exceptions with material regulatory or financial exposure. Approvers may not authorize exceptions to policies for which they are the requesting party.

items.name: Compensating Controls
items.description: Where an exception weakens a control objective, the approval must identify compensating controls that hold residual risk within tolerance for the exception's duration, such as added monitoring, secondary review, or restricted scope. The effectiveness of compensating controls is validated as part of granting and renewing the exception.

items.name: Exception Request Process
items.description: Any deviation from an approved corporate policy must be requested through the formal exception process, documenting the policy provision affected, the business justification, the risk introduced, and the requested duration. Verbal or undocumented exceptions are not recognized, and operating outside policy without an approved exception is treated as a compliance violation.

items.name: Owner Assigned
items.description: Each policy has a designated owner of appropriate seniority who is accountable for its content, its alignment with current regulation and business practice, and the timeliness of its reviews. Ownership is reassigned promptly upon departures or reorganizations so no policy is left orphaned.

items.name: Policy Inventory
items.description: A complete inventory of all corporate policies is maintained in a central repository, recording each policy's title, owner, applicable business areas, regulatory drivers, and review status. The inventory is the authoritative catalog; policies not registered in it are not recognized as effective.

items.name: Review Cycle (Annual Minimum)
items.description: Every policy is reviewed no less than annually, and sooner when regulatory change, audit findings, or operational shifts make its content stale. Reviews confirm continued accuracy and relevance, and the review date, reviewer, and outcome are recorded in the inventory.

items.name: Time-Limited
items.description: Every approved exception carries an explicit expiration date, after which the business must either return to compliance or submit a fresh request with updated justification. Standing or open-ended exceptions are prohibited, and the exception register is reviewed regularly to catch items approaching expiry.

items.name: Version Control
items.description: Policy documents are maintained under version control that preserves prior versions, records what changed and who approved it, and ensures only the current approved version is published to employees. Historical versions remain retrievable to support examinations, litigation holds, and investigations into past conduct.

items.name: Applicable Regulations Catalogued
items.description: All laws, regulations, and binding guidance applicable to the company's licensed entities, product lines, and jurisdictions are catalogued in a structured inventory, spanning state insurance codes, NAIC model adoptions, and applicable federal requirements such as privacy and anti-money laundering rules. Each entry records the obligation's substance and the business activities it touches.

items.name: Changes Tracked
items.description: The inventory is updated as regulations are adopted, amended, or repealed, drawing on the regulatory change management process, with each entry's revision history preserved. Updates trigger notification to the assigned owner so downstream policies, procedures, and controls are revisited.

items.name: Document Request Tracking
items.description: Every examiner request is logged with its receipt date, assigned owner, due date, and delivery status, giving the exam coordinator a single view of outstanding items. Productions are quality-checked for completeness and responsiveness before release, and a record of exactly what was provided is retained.

items.name: Exam Prep Protocol
items.description: A documented protocol governs readiness for state insurance department examinations, designating an exam coordinator, briefing affected business areas, staging commonly requested materials, and conducting readiness reviews in known problem areas before fieldwork begins. The protocol covers financial, market conduct, and targeted exams alike.

items.name: Findings Tracked to Closure
items.description: Every finding from an examination, inquiry, or enforcement action is entered into the regulatory issue register with an accountable owner, corrective action plan, and committed completion date, and remains open until remediation is verified, not merely reported. Closure requires evidence sufficient to demonstrate the fix to the regulator if requested.

items.name: Impact Assessments Performed
items.description: Applicable regulatory changes receive a documented impact assessment identifying affected products, processes, systems, forms, and policies, the compliance deadline, and the scale of effort required. Assessments are completed with enough lead time for the business to plan implementation ahead of the effective date.

items.name: Implementation Tracked
items.description: Required changes are assigned to accountable business owners with milestones tracked through to completion, including system updates, form refilings, procedure revisions, and staff training. Status is reported to compliance leadership, and items at risk of missing their regulatory effective date are escalated for intervention.

items.name: Ownership Assigned
items.description: Every catalogued obligation is mapped to a business or compliance owner responsible for ensuring the company's processes and controls satisfy it. Ownership mappings are validated periodically so coverage gaps created by reorganizations or new products are caught and reassigned.

items.name: Preventive Measures
items.description: Beyond correcting the specific instance cited, remediation must include measures that prevent recurrence, such as control enhancements, monitoring additions, or procedure and training changes, applied across all business units and jurisdictions where the same condition could exist. The effectiveness of preventive measures is checked through subsequent compliance testing.

items.name: Regulatory Alerts Monitored
items.description: Designated staff monitor legislative activity, NAIC model law developments, state bulletins, and federal rulemaking through subscription services and regulator channels, capturing relevant items in a change log. Each alert is triaged for applicability to the company's licensed lines and jurisdictions within a defined intake window.

items.name: Response Review Process
items.description: Written responses to examiner inquiries, draft findings, and report comments undergo review by compliance and, where warranted, legal counsel before submission, ensuring accuracy, consistency with prior representations, and appropriate tone. Significant proposed responses, particularly those contesting findings, require sign-off at a designated senior level.

items.name: Root Cause Analysis
items.description: Each significant finding undergoes analysis to determine the underlying cause, distinguishing isolated execution errors from defects in process design, system logic, training, or oversight. The analysis is documented and shapes the corrective action so the response addresses the cause rather than the symptom.

items.name: Accuracy Controls
items.description: Filings are subject to defined preparation controls, including reconciliation of reported figures to source systems and the general ledger, independent review by someone other than the preparer, and sign-off by the accountable officer where attestation is required. Errors discovered post-submission are corrected through the prescribed amendment process and analyzed for cause.

items.name: Filing Inventory
items.description: A master inventory lists every required regulatory filing across all jurisdictions and licensed entities, including statutory financial statements, market conduct annual statements, premium tax returns, and state data calls, with each filing's frequency, due date, preparer, and reviewer. New obligations identified through regulatory change management are added before their first due date.

items.name: Retention Requirements
items.description: Submitted filings, supporting workpapers, and evidence of submission are retained in accordance with the corporate retention schedule and applicable state requirements, in a form that allows prompt retrieval during examinations or inquiries. Retention applies equally to superseded and amended versions so the full filing history is preserved.

items.name: Timely Submission
items.description: Each filing must be submitted on or before its regulatory deadline, with the calendar of due dates monitored and internal milestones set ahead of each deadline to absorb preparation slippage. Anticipated delays are escalated early enough to request extensions where the jurisdiction permits, and any late filing is logged and reported to compliance leadership.

items.name: Contract Requirements
items.description: Vendor contracts must include the protective provisions appropriate to the relationship's risk tier, such as confidentiality and data protection obligations, breach notification timeframes, audit and examination rights extending to insurance regulators, subcontracting restrictions, and termination remedies. Contract templates are maintained with legal, and deviations from required clauses follow the exception process.

items.name: Ongoing Monitoring
items.description: Active vendor relationships are monitored on a cadence set by their risk tier, including periodic reassessments, review of SOC reports and security attestations, performance against service levels, and tracking of vendor incidents and breaches. Deteriorating vendors are escalated, with remediation required or exit plans invoked when risk exceeds tolerance.

items.name: Risk Tiering
items.description: Each third party is assigned a risk tier based on criteria such as access to nonpublic personal information, performance of regulated functions like claims administration, criticality to operations, and concentration exposure. The tier drives the depth of due diligence, contract provisions, and ongoing monitoring applied to the relationship.

items.name: Vendor Due Diligence
items.description: Prospective vendors undergo risk-proportionate due diligence before engagement, evaluating financial stability, information security posture, regulatory and licensing status, business continuity capability, and use of subcontractors. Due diligence results are documented and must support an approval decision before contracts are executed or data is shared.

items.name: Bias Testing
items.description: Models that influence underwriting, pricing, or claims outcomes are tested for disparate impact across protected classes and proxy variables before approval. Testing methodology and results are retained as evidence for state insurance regulators, and identified disparities must be remediated or formally risk-accepted before deployment.

items.name: Drift Detection
items.description: Production models must be instrumented to detect statistical drift in both input features and output score distributions relative to the training baseline. Detection thresholds are set per model at deployment, and alerts route to the owning data science team so shifts in policyholder mix, claims patterns, or market conditions are caught early.

items.name: Explainability Requirements
items.description: Each model must meet an explainability bar appropriate to its use: adverse-action and rating models require reason codes or feature attributions that can be communicated to policyholders and regulators. Black-box techniques are permissible only where a documented interpretability method accompanies them.

items.name: Holdout Validation
items.description: Model performance must be demonstrated on a holdout dataset that was excluded from training and tuning, with results compared against the development sample to detect overfitting. The holdout design, including any time-based splits appropriate for policy and claims data, is documented in the validation report.

items.name: Model Development Lifecycle
items.description: Every predictive or analytical model follows a documented lifecycle spanning problem definition, data preparation, modeling, validation, deployment, and ongoing monitoring. This end-to-end discipline ensures models used in pricing, underwriting, claims, and fraud detection are traceable from business question to production behavior and can withstand model risk and regulatory scrutiny.

items.name: Model Risk Review
items.description: Before production release, every model receives an independent review under the enterprise model risk framework, covering conceptual soundness, data lineage, assumptions, and limitations. The review assigns a risk tier that dictates the depth of ongoing monitoring and the revalidation cycle.

items.name: Performance Metrics Tracked
items.description: Each model's agreed performance measures, such as accuracy, lift, calibration, or loss-ratio impact, are computed on a defined cadence and recorded in the model inventory. Results are reviewed against the benchmarks established at validation, with trends visible to model owners and the model risk function.

items.name: Retraining Triggers Defined
items.description: Every production model carries documented criteria that mandate retraining or recalibration, including performance falling below threshold, sustained drift, or material business changes such as new product launches or regulatory rate filings. Triggered retraining follows the full development lifecycle rather than ad hoc refits.

items.name: Certified Datasets for Self-Service
items.description: Self-service analysis is performed against datasets that the Data & Analytics team has certified for accuracy, definitions, and refresh reliability. Certification status is visible in the BI tools, and certified content covering policy, claims, billing, and distribution data is the default starting point for business analysts.

items.name: Consistent Design Language
items.description: Dashboards follow the enterprise BI style guide, including the approved color palette, typography, KPI tile layouts, and standard chart types for measures like loss ratio, premium, and claims frequency. Visual conventions carry the same meaning everywhere, so a red indicator on a P&C dashboard reads the same as on a Life & Retirement one.

items.name: Data Validation
items.description: Report figures are reconciled against source systems and, where applicable, against established financial or actuarial controls before release. Validation evidence, including tie-outs of premium, reserve, and claims totals, is retained with the report's documentation.

items.name: Drill-Down Capability
items.description: Summary views must let users navigate from enterprise or line-of-business aggregates down to the underlying detail, such as moving from book-level loss ratio to region, product, and individual claim. Drill paths are designed deliberately and preserve filter context at each level.

items.name: Governed Data Sources Only
items.description: Self-service content may connect only to approved, governed sources such as the certified semantic layer and warehouse schemas. Direct connections to operational systems, personal extracts, and unmanaged spreadsheets are prohibited as report sources, preventing shadow reporting of premium or loss figures.

items.name: Mobile-Friendly
items.description: Dashboards must render usably on tablets and phones, with responsive layouts or purpose-built mobile views for content consumed by field staff, agents, and traveling executives. Touch targets, legibility, and load behavior on mobile networks are verified before publication.

items.name: Performance Under 5 Second Load
items.description: Initial dashboard render must complete within five seconds under typical user load, validated during UAT and re-checked after material data model changes. Developers achieve this through aggregation tables, query tuning, and caching rather than by trimming required content.

items.name: Refresh Schedule Defined
items.description: Each production report declares its refresh cadence, data-as-of timing, and dependencies on upstream pipeline completion. The schedule is published to consumers so users of month-end financial or daily claims reports know exactly how current the data is.

items.name: Requirements Documented
items.description: Every report begins with written requirements capturing the business question, intended audience, source data, calculations, and any regulatory context such as statutory or NAIC reporting obligations. Requirements are approved by the requesting business owner before development starts.

items.name: Training Required
items.description: Users must complete the prescribed enablement curriculum, covering tool usage, data interpretation, and handling of confidential policyholder data, before receiving self-service authoring rights. Access is provisioned only after training completion is recorded.

items.name: UAT Sign-Off
items.description: The business owner must formally accept the report in user acceptance testing, confirming figures, filters, and layout against the documented requirements. Sign-off is recorded, and no report enters production distribution without it.

items.name: All Datasets Registered
items.description: Every dataset in the warehouse, lake, and approved analytical stores must be registered in the enterprise catalog, including its description, owner, and source. New datasets are registered as part of the deployment process, so nothing reaches production undocumented.

items.name: Business Glossary Terms Linked
items.description: Catalog entries are linked to approved business glossary terms, such as earned premium, incurred loss, or surrender rate, so technical fields map to a single agreed business meaning. Glossary stewardship resolves conflicting definitions across P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits usage.

items.name: Lineage Captured
items.description: End-to-end lineage from source systems through transformation pipelines to reports is recorded in the catalog, automatically where tooling allows. Lineage supports impact analysis for changes and gives auditors and regulators a defensible trace of how reported figures are produced.

items.name: Ownership, Classification, and Refresh Frequency Documented
items.description: Every dataset's metadata must record its accountable owner, its sensitivity classification under the enterprise scheme, and how often it is refreshed. These three attributes drive access decisions, privacy handling for policyholder data, and consumer expectations about currency, and they are verified during periodic catalog reviews.

items.name: Searchable
items.description: The catalog must support search across names, descriptions, glossary terms, and tags so users can locate relevant data without insider knowledge. Search quality is maintained through metadata completeness checks and periodic curation of stale or duplicate entries.

items.name: Technical and Business Metadata Required
items.description: Each asset carries both technical metadata, such as schema, data types, source system, and load mechanics, and business metadata, such as plain-language descriptions and glossary linkage. Both layers are mandatory at registration; an asset with only one is considered incomplete.

items.name: Audit Columns in All Tables
items.description: Every managed table carries standard audit columns recording load timestamp, source identifier, and pipeline or batch ID, populated automatically by the ingestion framework. These columns make any record's provenance traceable, supporting reconciliation, regulatory inquiries, and incident investigation.

items.name: Change Data Capture for Real-Time
items.description: Where near-real-time data is required, such as claims status feeds or fraud-screening inputs, pipelines use change data capture from source databases rather than high-frequency batch polling.
