CDC implementations must handle deletes and schema changes and are monitored for replication lag.

items.name: Data Contracts Enforced
items.description: Each pipeline validates inbound data against an agreed contract covering schema, types, nullability, and key constraints, negotiated with the producing system team. Contract violations quarantine the offending records or halt the load per the feed's criticality, rather than silently propagating bad data downstream.

items.name: ELT Preferred
items.description: Pipelines should land data in the platform first and transform it there, exploiting the warehouse and lake engines rather than external transformation servers. Traditional ETL is used only where justified, such as source-side filtering of sensitive policyholder attributes, and the exception is documented.

items.name: File Formats (Parquet/Delta)
items.description: Persisted lake data uses Parquet, with Delta Lake required where ACID updates, merges, or time travel are needed, such as for CDC targets and Silver conformed tables. Other formats are permitted only transiently in Bronze landing zones for source fidelity.

items.name: Idempotent
items.description: Pipelines must produce the same result when rerun for the same period or batch, using merge logic, deterministic keys, or overwrite-by-partition patterns. This allows operators to safely replay failed loads of premium, claims, or billing data without creating duplicates.

items.name: Incremental Loads
items.description: Recurring loads must process only new or changed records, using watermarks, change tracking, or comparable mechanisms, rather than full reloads of policy and claims history. Full refreshes are reserved for initial loads and documented recovery scenarios.

items.name: Medallion Architecture (Bronze/Silver/Gold)
items.description: Lake content is organized into Bronze raw ingestion, Silver cleansed and conformed, and Gold business-ready layers, with defined promotion criteria between each. Consumers other than engineering teams work from Silver or Gold; raw Bronze data is never exposed directly to reporting or self-service.

items.name: Monitoring and Alerting
items.description: Production pipelines emit run status, duration, row counts, and data freshness metrics to the central monitoring platform, with alerts routed to the on-call engineer on failure or SLA breach. Alert thresholds reflect downstream commitments, such as month-end close and regulatory reporting deadlines.

items.name: Partitioning Strategy
items.description: Each dataset declares a partitioning scheme appropriate to its access patterns, typically by ingestion or business date and, where useful, by line of business or source system. Partition design is reviewed at onboarding to prevent small-file proliferation and full-table scans on large policy and claims histories.

items.name: Schema Evolution Handled
items.description: Pipelines must tolerate additive source schema changes, such as new columns from a policy administration upgrade, without failing, and must fail loudly with clear diagnostics on breaking changes. The handling approach for each feed is documented alongside its data contract.

items.name: Accountability Documented
items.description: The specific duties of each owner and steward, including access approval, quality remediation, classification, and glossary maintenance, are written into role charters acknowledged by the assignees. Documentation makes accountability auditable when regulators or internal audit examine data handling for policyholder information.

items.name: Annual Review
items.description: Ownership assignments are reconfirmed at least annually, with reassignments triggered immediately by departures or reorganizations rather than waiting for the cycle. The review also verifies that owners have actively discharged their duties, such as completing access recertifications, during the period.

items.name: Approved by Data Council
items.description: New policies and material revisions take effect only after formal Data Council approval, recorded in Council minutes. This single approval authority prevents divergent line-of-business rules for the same data handling question.

items.name: Communicated Organization-Wide
items.description: Approved policies are published in the central policy repository and communicated to all affected staff through announcements and role-appropriate training. Policies carrying compliance obligations, such as PII handling, require tracked acknowledgment from employees with access to the relevant data.

items.name: Data Council Meets Monthly
items.description: A cross-functional Data Council, with representation from P&C, Life & Retirement, group benefits, IT, compliance, and actuarial, convenes monthly to approve policies, prioritize data initiatives, and adjudicate cross-domain issues. Minutes and decisions are recorded and published to stakeholders.

items.name: Escalation Path Defined
items.description: A documented escalation route carries unresolved data disputes from stewards to domain owners to the Data Council, with defined response timeframes at each tier. Issues with regulatory or financial-reporting exposure may be fast-tracked directly to the Council chair.

items.name: Every Dataset Has Assigned Owner and Steward
items.description: Each registered dataset names a business data owner accountable for its content and access decisions, and a data steward responsible for day-to-day quality and definition upkeep. Ownership is assigned at dataset onboarding and recorded in the catalog; unowned datasets are flagged for remediation or retirement.

items.name: Policies for Access, Retention, Quality, and Privacy
items.description: The enterprise maintains current written policies covering data access control, retention and disposal, quality management, and privacy protection, addressing obligations such as state insurance data security laws and privacy statutes. Each policy names its owner and review cycle, and gaps identified by audit or regulation drive prompt updates.

items.name: Roles, Responsibilities, and Policies Documented
items.description: The framework document defines each governance role, including data owners, stewards, custodians, and the chief data officer, with explicit responsibilities, and indexes the full set of enterprise data policies. The document is version-controlled and reviewed when organizational or regulatory changes occur.

items.name: Change Control Process
items.description: Additions, modifications, and retirements of reference values follow a documented request and approval workflow involving the affected data stewards, with changes communicated to consuming system owners ahead of release. Emergency changes are permitted with retroactive approval and documentation.

items.name: Code Tables Centrally Managed
items.description: All shared reference data is mastered in the central reference data repository, which is the sole authoritative source from which consuming systems subscribe or replicate. Industry code sets, such as NAIC and ISO classifications, are loaded and maintained centrally rather than keyed independently by each team.

items.name: Golden Record Rules Defined
items.description: For each mastered domain, documented rules specify which attributes constitute the golden record and which sources are authoritative for each, such as the policy administration system for coverage data and CRM for contact preferences. Rules are owned by the domain's data steward and versioned as sources change.

items.name: Match and Merge Logic Documented
items.description: The deterministic and probabilistic matching criteria used to identify the same customer, household, or producer across systems, along with merge thresholds and manual review bands, are fully documented and tuned against measured false-match rates. Changes to matching logic require steward approval and regression testing, since over-merging policyholder records carries privacy and servicing risk.

items.name: No Local Overrides
items.description: Consuming applications and reports may not redefine, extend, or remap centrally managed codes locally. Where a system needs an additional value, the request goes through central change control, so a cause-of-loss or product code means the same thing in every claims report and regulatory filing.

items.name: Survivorship Rules
items.description: When merged records conflict, documented survivorship rules determine which value wins per attribute, based on source trust ranking, recency, and completeness. The rules are implemented in the MDM hub rather than applied ad hoc, and overridden values remain traceable to their originating source.

items.name: Versioned
items.description: Reference datasets carry version identifiers and effective dates, and historical versions remain retrievable so that past reports and rate calculations can be reproduced against the codes in force at the time. Consumers can pin to a version or track the current one explicitly.

items.name: Access Logged
items.description: All access to PII-bearing datasets is logged with user identity, timestamp, and data accessed, and logs are retained per the audit policy and protected from tampering. Access patterns are reviewed for anomalies, supporting both insider-threat detection and the evidence requirements of privacy regulators.

items.name: All Data Classified (Public/Internal/Confidential/Restricted)
items.description: Every dataset, report, and extract is assigned one of the four enterprise sensitivity tiers at creation or onboarding, with classification criteria defined in the data classification policy. Policyholder PII, claims medical details, and underwriting files default to Confidential or Restricted, and unclassified data is treated as Confidential until assessed.

items.name: Automated Purge Where Possible
items.description: Systems and data stores implement automated deletion or archival jobs aligned to the retention schedule, with execution logs retained as evidence of disposal. Where automation is infeasible, a documented manual purge procedure with attestation applies, and the gap is tracked for remediation.

items.name: Encryption and Masking Applied
items.description: PII is encrypted at rest and in transit, and direct identifiers are masked, tokenized, or pseudonymized in non-production environments and in analytical datasets where the identifier is not required. Masking standards specify approved techniques per element, so SSNs and bank details never appear in clear text outside controlled production use.

items.name: Labeling Enforced
items.description: Classification labels are applied through catalog metadata and, where tooling supports it, embedded sensitivity labels on files and reports, and downstream controls such as access policies, masking, and DLP rules key off those labels. Periodic scans verify that labels exist and match the actual content, with mismatches routed to data stewards for correction.

items.name: Legal Hold Process
items.description: A defined process suspends purge for data subject to litigation, regulatory examination, or claims disputes, with holds recorded centrally and propagated to every system housing the affected records. Holds are released only on instruction from Legal, after which normal retention resumes.

items.name: PII Inventory Maintained
items.description: A current inventory records every dataset and system containing PII, the specific elements held, such as SSN, date of birth, health information, and financial details, and the lawful purpose for holding them. The inventory is updated as part of dataset onboarding and feeds privacy impact assessments and breach-response scoping.

items.name: Retention Enforced
items.description: PII is held no longer than the retention schedule permits, with purge and anonymization applied to identifiers even where aggregate records are kept longer for actuarial analysis. Compliance is verified through periodic sampling of PII stores against the schedule.

items.name: Retention Schedules by Data Type
items.description: A maintained retention schedule assigns keep periods to each data category, reflecting state insurance record-retention regulations, statutes of limitation for claims, and contractual obligations across P&C, life, and group benefits products. The schedule is owned jointly with Legal and Compliance and reviewed when regulations change.

items.name: Accuracy Above 99%
items.description: More than 99 percent of records must pass accuracy checks, validated through reconciliation to authoritative sources and conformance rules, such as premium amounts tying to the billing system and policy statuses matching administration systems. Accuracy is sampled and certified for datasets feeding financial and regulatory reporting.

items.name: Automated Profiling
items.description: Quality rules execute automatically on a defined cadence through the data quality platform, profiling datasets as they are loaded rather than relying on manual spot checks. New datasets are baseline-profiled at onboarding to set expectations before rules are formalized.

items.name: Completeness Above 99%
items.description: Critical data elements in governed datasets must be populated for more than 99 percent of records, measured by automated completeness rules against each dataset's defined critical fields. Datasets falling below the threshold are flagged on quality dashboards and enter remediation.

items.name: Data Quality Rules Defined by Data Domain
items.description: Stewards for each domain, such as policy, claims, billing, customer, and producer data, define the completeness, validity, consistency, and uniqueness rules that matter for their data, including insurance-specific checks like valid coverage effective dates and reconciled premium amounts. Rules are documented in the quality tool with business rationale and thresholds.

items.name: Data Quality Scores Published
items.description: Rule results roll up into quality scores per dataset and domain, published on dashboards visible to data owners, stewards, and consumers, including surfacing scores in the data catalog. Trends are reviewed in governance forums, and persistently low scores trigger remediation plans.

items.name: Issues Logged in Tracking System
items.description: Every identified data issue, whether found by automated quality checks, report consumers, or auditors, is recorded in the enterprise tracking system with severity, affected datasets, business impact, and an assigned owner. Verbal or email-only reporting does not count as logged, and issue aging is reviewed by data stewards.

items.name: Prevention Measures Implemented
items.description: Each completed root cause analysis produces preventive actions, such as new validation rules, data contract changes, or source-system fixes, with owners and due dates tracked to closure. Recurrence of a previously analyzed issue triggers escalation to the responsible domain owner.

items.name: Remediation Within 24 Hours
items.description: When a dataset breaches its completeness, accuracy, or timeliness target, remediation must begin and the issue be resolved or formally triaged with a communicated plan within 24 hours. Consumers of the affected data are notified promptly so downstream decisions and reports are not made on known-bad data.

items.name: Root Cause Analysis
items.description: Issues above the defined severity threshold receive a documented root cause analysis tracing the defect to its origin, such as a source system entry gap, pipeline transformation error, or broken business process. The analysis distinguishes the immediate correction of affected records from the underlying cause.

items.name: Timeliness Per Business SLA
items.description: Each governed dataset carries an agreed availability deadline, such as daily claims data by 7 a.m. or month-end financial data within the close calendar, negotiated with its business consumers. Pipeline monitoring measures actual delivery against these commitments and reports breaches.

items.name: Automated Deployment to Dev on Merge
items.description: Merging to the integration branch automatically deploys the build to the shared development environment without manual steps. This keeps the dev environment continuously current so downstream teams, including QA and integration partners, always test against the latest merged code.

items.name: Blue-Green or Canary Deployments
items.description: Production releases must use either a blue-green cutover or a canary rollout; direct in-place replacement of running services is not permitted. Canary releases route a small percentage of live traffic to the new version and are promoted only after error rates and latency remain within agreed thresholds, protecting quoting, billing, and claims traffic from untested code.

items.name: Builds Under 15 Minutes
items.description: The standard CI build, from trigger to pass-or-fail signal, must complete in under fifteen minutes. Teams whose builds exceed the limit are expected to parallelize stages, cache dependencies, or split slow suites, because long builds discourage frequent integration and delay defect detection.

items.name: CI Pipeline for All Repositories
items.description: Every active repository, including internal tools and batch jobs supporting actuarial and finance processes, must have a continuous integration pipeline that compiles the code and runs its test suite on each push. Repositories without a pipeline may not receive production deployments.

items.name: Consistent Dev, Test, and Prod Environments
items.description: Development, test, and production environments must run the same operating system images, runtime versions, middleware, and network topology, differing only in scale and data. Any intentional deviation is documented and reviewed, because behavior that cannot be reproduced in test cannot be certified for release to systems handling policy and claims data.

items.name: Externalized Configuration
items.description: Environment-specific values, including connection strings, endpoints, and credentials, must live outside the application artifact in a configuration service or secrets vault. The same immutable build is promoted through every environment, so what was tested is byte-for-byte what runs in production.

items.name: Feature Flags for Gradual Rollout
items.description: New functionality ships dark behind feature flags and is enabled progressively by segment, such as a single state, product line, or agent cohort. Flags must be managed in the approved flag platform with named owners and removal dates, so the codebase does not accumulate permanent toggles.

items.name: Infrastructure as Code for All Environments
items.description: Every environment is provisioned exclusively from version-controlled infrastructure-as-code templates such as Terraform or CloudFormation; manual console changes are prohibited and detected via drift checks. This gives auditors and engineers a single reviewable definition of how each environment is built.

items.name: Instant Rollback Capability
items.description: Every deployment must be reversible within minutes through an automated rollback path that is tested as part of the release pipeline, not improvised during an incident. Database migrations accompanying a release are required to be backward compatible for at least one version so the prior build can be restored without data repair.

items.name: Quality Gates
items.description: Requires the CI pipeline to fail the build automatically whenever any test fails, code coverage drops below its threshold, a security scan reports a finding of High severity or above, or lint errors are present. No build that trips a gate may be promoted or manually overridden without a documented exception, ensuring code reaching insurance production systems has cleared a consistent, non-negotiable quality bar.

items.name: Addressed Within Two Sprints
items.description: Newly incurred debt items must be scheduled and remediated within two sprints of being raised. Items that cannot meet that window require an explicit deferral decision from the team lead, recorded on the backlog item, so debt is never silently abandoned.

items.name: Class Length Under 500 Lines
items.description: Classes may not exceed five hundred lines. Larger classes, frequently found in legacy policy administration adapters, must be refactored into focused collaborators rather than continually extended, preventing the god-object pattern from re-emerging.

items.name: Complex Logic Commented
items.description: Genuinely intricate logic, such as premium calculation formulas, reinsurance allocation rules, or state-specific regulatory branching, must carry comments explaining the business rationale and citing the source requirement or filing where applicable. The comment records why the code behaves as it does, not a line-by-line narration.

items.name: Consistent Formatting via Prettier or Black
items.description: Source formatting is applied automatically by an opinionated formatter, Prettier for JavaScript and TypeScript codebases and Black for Python, typically via pre-commit hooks. Hand-formatted variations are overwritten by the tool, guaranteeing that diffs show substantive changes only.

items.name: Cyclomatic Complexity Under 10
items.description: No method may exceed a cyclomatic complexity of ten, measured by static analysis in the pipeline. Branch-heavy logic, common in underwriting eligibility and claims adjudication code, must be decomposed into smaller decision units that can each be exhaustively tested.

items.name: Debt Ratio Below 15 Percent of Velocity
items.description: Teams allocate capacity so that outstanding debt remediation never demands more than fifteen percent of sprint velocity. When the ratio trends toward the ceiling, feature intake is throttled until the balance is restored, keeping delivery speed sustainable across long-lived policy and claims platforms.

items.name: Language-Specific Style Guides Enforced via Linters
items.description: Each approved language has a designated style guide, and conformance is enforced by linters such as ESLint or Checkstyle running in the CI pipeline. Lint violations fail the build, so stylistic conventions are applied mechanically rather than negotiated in review comments.

items.name: Method Length Under 50 Lines
items.description: Methods are limited to fifty lines of executable code. A method approaching the limit usually carries more than one responsibility and should be split, keeping each unit small enough for a reviewer to verify in a single reading.

items.name: No Commented-Out Code in Main Branch
items.description: Disabled code blocks must not be committed to the main branch; version control history is the mechanism for recovering removed code. Reviewers are expected to reject pull requests containing commented-out fragments, which obscure the active logic and mislead future maintainers.

items.name: Self-Documenting Code Preferred
items.description: Engineers should express intent through descriptive names, small functions, and clear structure before reaching for a comment. A comment that merely restates what the code does signals the code itself should be rewritten for clarity.

items.name: SonarQube Gates Enforced
items.description: These thresholds are codified as SonarQube quality gates wired into CI, so a violation fails the build rather than relying on reviewer vigilance. Gate configurations are managed centrally and teams may tighten, but not loosen, them without an approved exception.

items.name: Tech Debt Tagged in Backlog
items.description: Every known piece of technical debt must be captured as a backlog item with a standard debt tag, a description of the compromise made, and an estimate of remediation effort. Untracked debt discovered during development is logged at the time it is found, so the portfolio of debt is always visible to product owners and engineering leadership.

items.name: Constructive Feedback
items.description: Review comments address the code, never the author, and are expected to explain the reasoning behind a requested change or link to the relevant standard. Blocking comments are distinguished from optional suggestions so authors know exactly what must change before merge.

items.name: Functionality, Tests, Security, Performance, and Maintainability Checked
items.description: Reviewers must work through the standard checklist on every pull request, confirming the change does what the work item requires, carries adequate tests, introduces no security weaknesses such as injection paths or exposure of policyholder data, performs acceptably at production volumes, and remains readable for future maintainers. Approval attests that each dimension was considered, not merely that the code compiles.

items.name: No PR Open Beyond 48 Hours Without Action
items.description: No pull request may remain open for more than forty-eight hours without recorded activity, whether approval, requested changes, or an explicit hold note. Stale PRs are escalated to the team lead and surfaced on the engineering dashboard so aging work is resolved or consciously parked.

items.name: PRs Reviewed Within Four Hours
items.description: A submitted pull request must receive its first substantive review within four business hours. Teams are expected to treat review as a first-class daily duty, arranging coverage across time zones where squads are distributed, because stalled reviews block delivery of fixes to customer-facing insurance services.

items.name: Pairing Required for Complex Features
items.description: Features judged complex during sprint planning, including changes to rating engines, payment processing, or cross-system integrations, must be built by a pair rather than a solo engineer. The pairing requirement applies from design through implementation, giving every high-risk change two sets of eyes before it ever reaches formal review.

items.name: Weekly Knowledge Sharing Sessions
items.description: Each team holds a recurring weekly session in which engineers present recent designs, incident learnings, or unfamiliar areas of the codebase to colleagues. Sessions are recorded and indexed so that domain knowledge, particularly around legacy life and annuity systems, spreads beyond the individuals who currently maintain them.

items.name: Architecture Decision Records for Decisions
items.description: Significant technical decisions, such as selecting a policy administration integration pattern or adopting an event streaming platform, are captured as architecture decision records stored alongside the code. Each ADR states the context, the options weighed, the choice made, and its consequences, giving future teams the rationale they need before reversing or extending a decision.

items.name: C4 Diagrams Maintained
items.description: Every system maintains current C4 model diagrams covering at least the context and container levels, showing how it relates to surrounding platforms such as billing, document management, and data warehouses. Diagrams are stored as code where practical and reviewed whenever the architecture materially changes, so they remain a trustworthy reference rather than a stale artifact.

items.name: Changelog Maintained
items.description: API changes are recorded in a versioned changelog noting additions, deprecations, and breaking changes, with deprecations announced ahead of removal per the API versioning policy. Consumers inside and outside the company rely on the changelog to plan their own upgrade work.

items.name: Examples Provided
items.description: Each documented endpoint includes realistic request and response examples, using synthetic policy and claim data that mirrors production shapes without containing real customer information. Examples must cover common error responses as well as the success path so integrators can handle failures correctly.

items.name: Kept Current
items.description: README content is updated in the same pull request as the change that invalidates it, and accuracy is checked during onboarding and periodic repo health reviews. An outdated README is treated as a defect to be fixed, not an accepted state.

items.name: Onboarding Guide for New Developers
items.description: Each team keeps an onboarding guide that takes a new engineer from zero to a merged change, covering domain context, system landscape, access requests, and local setup. The guide is validated by each new joiner, who is expected to fix anything found out of date as their first contribution.

items.name: OpenAPI Spec Auto-Generated
items.description: Every HTTP API must publish an OpenAPI specification generated from source annotations or contract definitions as part of the build, never maintained by hand. The generated spec is the contract of record for consumers ranging from the mobile claims app to third-party agency management systems, and a build whose spec generation fails does not ship.

items.name: README Covers Purpose, Setup, Run, Test, and Deploy
items.description: Every repository must contain a README that states what the system does and which business capability it serves, then walks through environment setup, running locally, executing the test suite, and how deployment works. An engineer unfamiliar with the repo should be able to reach a running local instance using the README alone.

items.name: Actionable Alerts
items.description: Every alert must correspond to a condition that requires human action and indicate plainly what is failing and who is affected. Informational signals belong on dashboards, not pages; an alert that repeatedly fires without prompting action must be tuned or retired.

items.name: Alert Fatigue Monitored
items.description: Teams track paging volume, after-hours interruptions, and the ratio of actionable to non-actionable alerts as standing metrics reviewed in operational meetings. Sustained noise triggers a mandatory alert-tuning effort, because a desensitized on-call rotation will eventually miss the page that matters.

items.name: Appropriate Log Levels
items.description: Engineers apply severity levels by their defined meanings: ERROR for failures needing attention, WARN for degraded but functioning behavior, INFO for significant business events, and DEBUG for detail disabled in production by default. Disciplined leveling keeps production log volume manageable and makes severity-based filtering meaningful during incidents.

items.name: Correlation IDs
items.description: A correlation identifier is generated at the edge of each request and propagated through every downstream service, queue message, and batch handoff it touches. This allows a single customer transaction, such as a first notice of loss, to be traced end to end across the many systems that participate in it.

items.name: Dashboards per Service
items.description: Each production service has a maintained dashboard presenting its RED metrics, resource utilization, and key business indicators such as quotes issued or claims transactions processed. Dashboards follow a common layout so any responder can orient quickly in an unfamiliar service during an incident.

items.name: Distributed Tracing Enabled
items.description: Services participate in the platform-wide distributed tracing system, propagating trace context across HTTP calls, messaging, and scheduled jobs. Traces reveal where time is spent when a transaction crosses many systems, which is essential for diagnosing slowness in flows like quote-to-issue that traverse rating, underwriting, and document services.

items.name: No PII in Logs
items.description: Logs must never contain personally identifiable information, protected health information, or payment data; identifiers such as policy or claim numbers are used in place of names, and sensitive fields are masked at the logging framework level. Automated scanning of log streams checks for violations, which are treated as security incidents given the regulatory obligations on nonpublic personal information.

items.name: On-Call Rotation
items.description: Every production service is covered by a defined on-call rotation with documented schedules, handoff procedures, and escalation tiers. Rotations are staffed to keep individual load sustainable, and engineers joining a rotation must first complete shadow shifts.

items.name: RED Metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration)
items.description: Every service exposes request rate, error rate, and duration metrics as its baseline instrumentation, with latency captured as percentile distributions rather than averages. These three signals form the common health language used in service-level objectives and incident triage across all engineering teams.

items.name: Runbook Linked
items.description: Each alert definition carries a link to a runbook describing diagnosis steps, remediation options, and escalation contacts, including business escalation paths for incidents touching claims payments or policyholder data. Alerts without a runbook may not be promoted to production paging.

items.name: Structured JSON Logging
items.description: All services emit logs as structured JSON with standard fields for timestamp, service name, severity, and event details, rather than free-form text. Structured output lets the central log platform index and query events consistently across every system from quoting front ends to batch policy renewals.

items.name: 90 Percent Coverage for Critical Paths
items.description: Code paths with direct financial or compliance impact, including premium rating, claims payment calculation, commission processing, and regulatory reporting, are held to a ninety percent minimum. Teams designate these critical modules explicitly so the elevated gate is applied automatically where a defect could mean mispriced policies or incorrect payouts.

items.name: All Regression Automated
items.description: The full regression suite, covering established behavior such as rating accuracy, policy lifecycle transitions, and claims workflows, must be automated and executed in the pipeline. Manual regression passes are not an accepted release practice, since they cannot keep pace with the release cadence and silently shrink under deadline pressure.

items.name: Automated Regression Detection
items.description: Pipeline-integrated checks compare each candidate build's performance results against the baseline and flag statistically significant degradation automatically, rather than depending on someone noticing a slow graph. A detected regression must be resolved or formally accepted with justification before the release proceeds.

items.name: Contract Tests for APIs
items.description: Service interfaces are protected by consumer-driven contract tests, using tooling such as Pact, that verify a provider continues to satisfy the expectations of every registered consumer. Contract verification runs in CI on both sides, so a breaking change to a shared API, for example one consumed by both the agent portal and the mobile app, fails the build before it can be released.

items.name: Integration Tests for External Dependencies
items.description: Interactions with external systems, including MVR and credit bureau services, payment processors, reinsurers, and state regulatory interfaces, are covered by integration tests run against sandboxes or high-fidelity stubs. Tests must exercise failure modes such as timeouts and malformed responses, not just the happy path, because partner outages are a routine production reality.

items.name: Load Tests Before Production
items.description: Changes that could affect throughput or latency must pass load tests in a production-like environment before release, using traffic models that reflect peak conditions such as billing runs or a CAT event driving concentrated first-notice-of-loss volume. Results are compared against the service's capacity targets, and a failed load test blocks the release.

items.name: Manual Testing for Exploratory Only
items.description: Human testing is reserved for exploratory sessions: charter-driven investigation of new features, unusual policy and claim scenarios, and usability concerns that scripted checks cannot evaluate. Defects found during exploration are converted into automated tests so the same issue is guarded against permanently.

items.name: Minimum 80 Percent Line Coverage
items.description: Every codebase must sustain at least eighty percent line coverage from its unit suite, enforced as a pipeline gate that fails builds falling below the threshold. Coverage must come from meaningful assertions; tests written purely to inflate the number are rejected in review.

items.name: No Untested Public Methods
items.description: Every public method must be exercised by at least one unit test covering its primary behavior and principal error cases. A public surface with no tests is treated as unfinished work, since public methods are exactly the contracts other components depend on.

items.name: Performance Baseline Established
items.description: Each service maintains a recorded performance baseline covering latency percentiles, throughput, and resource consumption at reference load. The baseline is refreshed after significant releases and serves as the objective reference point for judging whether subsequent changes have helped or harmed.

items.name: Test Data Management
items.description: Integration suites run against governed synthetic test data that reflects realistic policy, customer, and claim structures; production data may not be copied into lower environments without approved masking. Test datasets are versioned and refreshable on demand so suites remain deterministic and repeatable.

items.name: Test Pyramid Observed
items.description: Suites are shaped according to the test pyramid, with fast unit tests forming the bulk of coverage, a moderate layer of integration tests, and a deliberately small set of end-to-end journeys such as quote-to-bind. Inverted pyramids dominated by slow UI tests are flagged in engineering health reviews and scheduled for rebalancing.

items.name: Atomic Commits
items.description: Each commit contains exactly one logical change that builds and passes tests on its own. Mixing a bug fix with an unrelated refactor in a single commit is not permitted, because atomic history makes review, bisection, and selective revert practical when a production issue must be isolated quickly.

items.name: CI Must Pass
items.description: Merge is blocked until all required pipeline checks, including tests, coverage, security scanning, and lint, complete successfully on the latest commit. Approvals do not override a red build, and bypassing checks requires a documented emergency exception.

items.name: Conventional Commits Format
items.description: Commit messages follow the Conventional Commits specification, beginning with a type such as feat, fix, or chore and an optional scope. The structured format is machine-parseable, enabling automated changelog generation and semantic version calculation across the engineering organization.

items.name: Feature Branches Under Three Days
items.description: A feature branch should live no longer than three working days before merging. Work too large for that window is decomposed into incremental slices, using feature flags to keep unfinished functionality dark, so branches stay small and merge conflicts stay rare.

items.name: GitFlow or Trunk-Based Development
items.description: Each repository adopts one of the two sanctioned models, GitFlow or trunk-based development, documents the choice in its README, and applies it consistently. Trunk-based flow is preferred for services on continuous delivery, while GitFlow remains acceptable for systems with scheduled release trains such as core policy administration.

items.name: Linked to Work Item
items.description: Every commit references its originating backlog item or defect identifier, validated by a server-side hook. The link provides end-to-end traceability from an approved piece of work to the exact code that implemented it, evidence routinely requested in change-management audits.

items.name: Meaningful Messages
items.description: Commit messages state what changed and why in terms a future maintainer can act on; placeholders like fixes or wip may not reach a protected branch. Where the motivation is not obvious, the message body explains the context, such as the regulatory bulletin or defect that prompted the change.

items.name: No Direct Commits to Main or Master
items.description: Commits may never be made directly to the main or master branch under any circumstances, including hotfixes, which follow an expedited pull request path instead. Combined with branch protection, this keeps review and CI as unconditional steps in the route to production.

items.name: No Force Push
items.description: Force pushes and branch deletion are disabled on protected branches so committed history is immutable. This guarantees the audit trail of changes to production systems cannot be altered after the fact, and corrections are made with new commits or reverts rather than rewrites.

items.name: Pull Request Required for Main and Develop
items.description: All changes to main and develop must arrive through a pull request; direct pushes are disabled at the platform level for every contributor, including administrators. The PR record preserves who changed what and why, forming part of the change-control audit trail.

items.name: Two Approvers Required
items.description: Merging requires approval from two reviewers who are not the author, with at least one holding code-owner responsibility for the affected area. The dual-approval rule ensures no single individual can move code into a protected branch unilaterally, a separation-of-duties control auditors verify.

items.name: ACORD code lists are version-current across systems
items.description: Every ACORD code list referenced by registered schemas and mapping specifications is pinned to a current ACORD code-list version so that enumerations remain interoperable across systems.

items.name: ACORD forms in use are on the current release version
items.description: Every ACORD form rendered, ingested, or filed by the organization is on the current ACORD release version so that downstream carriers, agents, and regulators receive standard-conformant document layouts.

items.name: ACORD transaction envelopes are well-formed and conformant
items.description: Every ACORD transaction exchanged over the integration platform is wrapped in a well-formed, conformant ACORD transaction envelope, so that routing, correlation, and acknowledgement metadata are reliably interpreted by partner endpoints.

items.name: Certificates of insurance use the current ACORD 25 form
items.description: Every certificate of liability insurance issued uses the current revision of the standard ACORD 25 form, so that certificate holders, agencies, and carriers exchange legally compliant, up-to-date certificates.

items.name: Internal data fields map to the ACORD data dictionary
items.description: Every internal data field that participates in carrier, agency, or regulatory exchange is mapped to a corresponding element in the ACORD data dictionary so that semantics are preserved across the integration estate.

items.name: Life & Annuity messages conform to ACORD TXLife
items.description: Every Life & Annuity message exchanged over the integration platform validates against the ACORD TXLife standard, so that new-business, in-force, and distribution partners exchange structurally conformant Life & Annuity transactions.

items.name: Life OLI_LU code lists are valid and current
items.description: Every coded value carried on a Life & Annuity message uses a valid OLI_LU code drawn from the current ACORD OLI code list, so that enumerated values are interpreted consistently across carriers, BGAs, and distribution platforms.

items.name: Mandatory ACORD data elements are populated on P&C messages
items.description: Every P&C message carries fully populated values for all data elements that the ACORD P&C Data Standard and Data Dictionary mark as mandatory, so that downstream carriers and analytics consumers receive complete, usable policy data.

items.name: Message schemas are registered and version-pinned
items.description: Every message schema used by policy and partner integrations is registered in the schema registry and pinned to an explicit version so that producers and consumers evolve compatibly.

items.name: P&C policy messages validate against the ACORD P&C XML schema
items.description: Every outbound and inbound P&C policy message exchanged over the integration platform validates cleanly against the published ACORD P&C XML (XSD) schema, so that carrier and agency partners receive structurally conformant transactions.

items.name: Policy APIs align to the ACORD reference model (ADAPT)
items.description: Every policy API endpoint exposed by the organization aligns to the ACORD reference model and the ACORD ADAPT API patterns so that partners can integrate against standard, predictable insurance entities.

items.name: Reinsurance messaging conforms to ACORD GRLC
items.description: Every reinsurance message exchanged with brokers, cedents, and reinsurers conforms to the ACORD Global Reinsurance and Large Commercial (GRLC) standard so that placements, bordereaux, and technical accounts process straight-through.

items.name: API Keys for Partners
items.description: External partners such as agencies, brokers, TPAs, and group-benefits platforms are issued individual API keys in addition to OAuth credentials, enabling per-partner identification, quota assignment, and revocation. Keys are provisioned through the partner onboarding process, rotated on a defined schedule, and never shared across organizations.

items.name: Auto-Generated From Code
items.description: Specifications are produced from source annotations or framework metadata as part of the build, rather than maintained by hand. This keeps documentation synchronized with deployed behavior and makes drift between the spec and the running service a build-time defect instead of a production surprise.

items.name: Breaking Changes Require Consumer Notification
items.description: Any change that removes fields, alters semantics, or tightens validation must be communicated to all registered consumers before release, with a documented migration window. Notification follows the API catalog's consumer registry, and release approval requires evidence that affected teams, including external distribution partners, have acknowledged the change.

items.name: Caching Headers
items.description: Responses declare explicit cache behavior through Cache-Control, ETag, and related headers, distinguishing safely cacheable reference data, like product or coverage catalogs, from volatile or sensitive resources that must not be cached. Conditional request support is expected wherever it materially reduces repeated payload transfer.

items.name: Compression Enabled
items.description: HTTP response compression, gzip at minimum, is enabled for compressible content types on all APIs. This reduces bandwidth and latency for large payloads such as policy documents metadata or claims search results, particularly for field adjusters and agents on constrained networks.

items.name: Consistent Error Codes
items.description: Error type identifiers and business error codes are drawn from a governed enterprise catalog, so the same condition, for example a lapsed policy or an ineligible coverage, maps to the same code across every API. New codes are registered centrally before use to prevent overlapping or duplicate meanings.

items.name: Consistent Naming Conventions
items.description: Resource paths, query parameters, and JSON field names follow the published enterprise naming standard, including casing rules, plural resource nouns, and approved domain vocabulary aligned with the corporate glossary. Insurance terms must be used consistently, so the same concept is never exposed as policyHolder in one API and insuredParty in another.

items.name: Consumer-Driven Contracts
items.description: API expectations are defined from the consumer's perspective, with each consuming team publishing a contract that captures the requests it makes and the response shapes it depends on. Provider teams treat the union of these contracts as the binding interface definition, ensuring that a policy administration API change cannot be considered safe until every registered consumer contract still holds.

items.name: Contract Testing in CI/CD
items.description: Every build of an API provider executes automated contract tests against the current set of consumer contracts, and consumer builds verify against the provider's published contract. A failed contract verification fails the pipeline, preventing deployment of changes that would break an integration partner such as a claims intake or agent portal service.

items.name: HATEOAS for Discoverability
items.description: Responses include hypermedia links that advertise valid next actions and related resources, such as a claim payload linking to its associated policy, payments, and permissible status transitions. This lets clients navigate workflows dynamically and reduces hardcoded URL construction in consuming applications.

items.name: Header Versioning for Minor Changes
items.description: Backward-compatible refinements may be selected through a version or media-type header rather than a new URI, keeping resource addresses stable. Minor versions must remain additive, so a consumer that ignores the header continues to receive a valid, compatible response.

items.name: Input Validation
items.description: All inbound parameters, headers, and payloads are validated against the API's schema and business rules before processing, rejecting malformed, oversized, or unexpected input. Validation occurs server-side regardless of any client checks, as a primary defense against injection attacks and data corruption in systems of record.

items.name: No PII in URLs
items.description: Personally identifiable information, including Social Security numbers, policy numbers tied to individuals, dates of birth, and health details, must never appear in URL paths or query strings, where it would persist in logs, browser histories, and proxies. Such data is conveyed only in request bodies or headers over encrypted channels, with opaque identifiers used for resource addressing.

items.name: No Stack Traces in Production
items.description: Production error responses must never include stack traces, internal class names, SQL fragments, or infrastructure details. Diagnostic context is written to centralized logging with a correlation identifier that is returned to the caller, allowing support teams to trace an incident without exposing internals to consumers or attackers.

items.name: OAuth 2.0 and OIDC
items.description: APIs are protected with OAuth 2.0 access tokens, with OpenID Connect used for user authentication and identity propagation. Scopes are defined per business capability so a consumer authorized to read claim status cannot invoke payment or policy-change operations, and token validation is enforced at the gateway as well as in the service.

items.name: OpenAPI 3.0 Specs Required
items.description: Each API must carry a complete OpenAPI 3.0 specification covering all endpoints, schemas, security schemes, and error responses. The specification is the authoritative interface description used for design review, contract testing, and partner onboarding, and an API without one cannot pass architecture review.

items.name: P95 Latency Under 200ms
items.description: APIs must serve the 95th percentile of requests in under 200 milliseconds, measured at the gateway under representative production load. Teams track this objective in their observability dashboards, and sustained breaches trigger performance remediation work before new feature delivery, since slow APIs directly degrade quoting and claims-intake experiences.

items.name: Pagination Required for Collections
items.description: Endpoints returning collections, such as policy lists, claim histories, or billing transactions, must paginate using the standard cursor or offset conventions with documented default and maximum page sizes. Unbounded result sets are prohibited because portfolio-scale queries can return millions of rows and destabilize both provider and consumer.

items.name: Published to Developer Portal
items.description: Generated specifications are published automatically to the enterprise developer portal, where they are versioned, searchable, and paired with usage guides and sandbox access. The portal is the single discovery point for all APIs, including those consumed by agency, broker, and group-benefits integration partners.

items.name: RESTful Design
items.description: APIs follow REST conventions over HTTPS, using standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) with their defined semantics and appropriate status codes. Operations must be modeled as state transfers on resources rather than remote procedure calls, so a quote, policy, or claim is manipulated through predictable, cacheable interactions.

items.name: RFC 7807 Problem Details Format
items.description: All error responses use the RFC 7807 Problem Details structure, returning application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail, and instance members. Domain-specific extensions, such as underwriting decline reasons or claim validation failures, are added as documented extension members rather than ad hoc payloads.

items.name: Rate Limiting
items.description: Every exposed API enforces request rate limits at the gateway, with per-consumer quotas tuned to legitimate usage patterns. Limits protect core systems like policy administration and claims platforms from abusive traffic, runaway integrations, and denial-of-service conditions, and limit breaches return the standard 429 response with retry guidance.

items.name: Resource-Oriented
items.description: Interfaces are organized around business resources such as policies, claims, insureds, and invoices, identified by stable URIs, rather than around internal system operations. Resource boundaries should reflect the insurance domain model, keeping URLs meaningful to integrators and decoupled from the implementing system's database structure.

items.name: Twelve-Month Deprecation Policy
items.description: When a version is deprecated, it remains supported for a minimum of twelve months, during which consumers receive deprecation headers, portal notices, and direct communication through the consumer registry. Retirement before the window closes requires ARB approval and confirmation that all remaining traffic has migrated.

items.name: URI Versioning for Breaking Changes
items.description: Breaking changes are released under a new major version segment in the URI, such as /v1 to /v2, leaving the prior version operational in parallel. This allows agency systems, vendor platforms, and internal consumers to migrate on their own schedules rather than being forced into lockstep releases.

items.name: ADRs Required for Significant Decisions
items.description: Any architecturally significant decision, such as selecting a policy administration integration pattern, adopting a new platform, or departing from a reference architecture, must be documented as an ADR before implementation proceeds. Each record states the context, the options considered, the decision, and its consequences in the standard template.

items.name: ARB Approval Required for Major Initiatives
items.description: Initiatives that exceed defined cost, risk, or cross-domain impact thresholds, including core system replacements, new vendor platforms, and material integration programs, must present to the ARB and obtain approval before funding gates are passed. Submissions use the standard solution architecture package so reviews compare like for like.

items.name: Approved Patterns Documented With Examples
items.description: Each reference architecture, covering areas such as API integration, event streaming, document management, and core-system extension, is documented with its intended context, component diagram, technology choices, and at least one worked example from a real implementation. Patterns are versioned and reviewed periodically so the library reflects current platforms rather than retired ones.

items.name: Automated Tests for Architecture Compliance
items.description: Teams encode architectural rules, such as dependency direction between layers, prohibited library usage, bounded-context isolation, and latency or coupling thresholds, as automated fitness functions. These tests make the intended architecture objectively measurable instead of relying on documentation and goodwill.

items.name: Decision Log Maintained
items.description: Every ARB outcome, including approvals, conditions, deferrals, and rejections, is recorded in a maintained decision log with rationale and owners for any follow-up actions. The log is accessible to delivery teams and auditors, and conditions are tracked to closure rather than forgotten after the meeting.

items.name: Detailed Design Reviewed by Peers
items.description: Detailed technical designs, covering component structure, data models, integration contracts, and failure handling, are reviewed by engineers and architects from outside the authoring team before build begins. Reviewers record findings and the author must resolve or formally accept each one, creating a documented quality gate below the solution-architecture level.

items.name: Deviations Require Justification and Approval
items.description: A solution that departs from an applicable reference architecture must record the business or technical justification and obtain approval through the architecture review process before build begins. Approved deviations are logged and revisited, since each one either signals a gap the library should absorb or a debt item to be remediated.

items.name: Failures Block Deployment
items.description: A failing fitness function is a hard gate; the pipeline stops and the change cannot be promoted until the violation is fixed or a documented, time-boxed exception is approved by the architecture function. This ensures compliance debt cannot silently accumulate in production insurance systems.

items.name: Run in CI/CD
items.description: Fitness functions execute in the continuous integration pipeline on every build, alongside unit and contract tests. Running them this early surfaces architectural erosion, like a claims service reaching directly into the policy database, at the moment it is introduced rather than during an annual review.

items.name: Security, Performance, and Operability Checklist
items.description: Each review works through the standard checklist covering security items such as authentication, authorization, and data protection for policyholder information, performance items such as expected volumes and latency budgets, and operability items such as logging, monitoring, alerting, and runbook readiness. The completed checklist is attached to the design artifact as evidence of the review.

items.name: Solution Architecture Document Required Before Development
items.description: No development effort beyond approved spikes may begin until a solution architecture document has been completed and reviewed. The document covers business context, component and integration views, data flows including any PII or PHI handling, non-functional requirements, and alignment with reference architectures, giving reviewers a full picture before code is written.

items.name: Standardized Template
items.description: All solution architecture documents use the enterprise template, which prescribes the required sections, diagram notations, and sign-off matrix. A common structure lets reviewers across the architecture community assess designs efficiently and makes documents comparable across the P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits portfolios.

items.name: Status Tracked Through Lifecycle
items.description: Every ADR carries an explicit status of Proposed, Accepted, or Deprecated, updated as the decision moves through review and is eventually superseded. A deprecated record is never deleted; it references the ADR that replaced it, preserving the chain of reasoning for auditors and future architects.

items.name: Stored in Repo
items.description: ADRs live in version control alongside the code or platform they govern, typically in a docs/adr directory, so they are diffable, reviewable through pull requests, and discoverable by the teams doing the work. Repository storage keeps the decision history coupled to the system's evolution rather than buried in shared drives.

items.name: Tech Debt Logged, Prioritized, and Scheduled
items.description: Identified debt items, from outdated frameworks in policy systems to shortcut integrations and missing test coverage, are recorded in the central register with a description, affected systems, risk rating, and estimated remediation effort. Items are prioritized against business risk and scheduled into delivery plans, so each entry carries an owner and a target rather than sitting as an unbounded backlog.

items.name: Twenty Percent Capacity Reserved for Debt Reduction
items.description: Delivery teams reserve roughly twenty percent of each planning increment for remediating items from the debt register. This allocation is protected during planning and tracked in increment reviews, preventing feature pressure from indefinitely deferring the maintenance that keeps quoting, claims, and billing platforms reliable.

items.name: Weekly Cadence
items.description: The board convenes weekly with a published agenda and quorum rules, keeping review latency short enough that governance does not stall delivery. Urgent items can be triaged between sessions through a documented expedited path, with the decision ratified at the next meeting.

items.name: Aggregation at the BFF Layer
items.description: Composition of data from multiple domain services, for example combining policy, billing, and claims status into a single account dashboard response, happens in the BFF rather than in the client or in core services. Domain APIs stay clean and reusable while each channel receives right-sized payloads in a single round trip.

items.name: Bounded Contexts Map to Teams
items.description: Each bounded context is owned end to end by a single long-lived team, and system boundaries are drawn so that a context does not span teams. Aligning ownership this way keeps models internally consistent, limits cross-team coordination on changes, and makes accountability for a domain like P&C claims or retirement servicing unambiguous.

items.name: Dedicated API Layer per Client Type
items.description: Each client category, including the policyholder web portal, mobile apps, and partner or agency channels, gets its own backend-for-frontend service shaped to that channel's screens and workflows. The BFF is owned by the team building the client experience, allowing channel-specific changes such as a mobile claims-photo flow without modifying shared domain APIs.

items.name: Event Sourcing Optional for Audit-Heavy Domains
items.description: Domains with intensive audit and reconstruction requirements, such as claims adjudication, policy endorsements, or financial postings, may additionally adopt event sourcing so state is derived from an immutable event log. The choice is optional and made per domain, weighing the regulatory value of a complete change history against the operational cost of event-store management and replay tooling.

items.name: Events for Cross-Domain Communication
items.description: When one domain needs to react to changes in another, for example billing responding to a policy issuance or analytics consuming claim status changes, the interaction is implemented through published domain events on the enterprise event backbone rather than synchronous point-to-point calls. Events follow the published schema standards and are treated as part of the producing domain's public contract.

items.name: Eventual Consistency Acceptable for Non-Financial Data
items.description: Consumers of events may lag the source of record briefly, and this eventual consistency is acceptable for non-financial data such as contact updates, document status, or dashboard aggregates. Financial movements, including premium collection, claim payments, and reserve changes, require stronger consistency guarantees and must not rely on eventually consistent projections for transactional decisions.

items.name: Gradual Cutover
items.description: Existing data and traffic are migrated in planned waves, with parallel-run validation, reconciliation checks, and rollback paths at each stage. The legacy system is decommissioned only after all functions and in-force records have been transitioned and verified, and the migration plan includes explicit exit criteria for each wave.

items.name: Independent Deployment
items.description: Every microservice is deployable on its own, with its own pipeline, versioning, and data store access, and without coordinated releases of other services. Designs that require lockstep deployment indicate hidden coupling and fail this criterion.

items.name: Legacy Modernization via Incremental Replacement
items.description: Legacy capabilities are replaced one slice at a time, with each slice, such as a product line's quoting or a specific claims workflow, rebuilt in the target architecture behind a routing facade. The legacy system keeps running throughout, and each increment must deliver verifiable, production-ready functionality before the next begins.

items.name: New Traffic to New System
items.description: Once a replaced capability is live, new business and new transactions are routed to the modern system while the legacy platform continues serving in-force business not yet migrated. The routing layer enforces this split deterministically, for example sending new policy issuance to the new core while renewals of unmigrated policies stay on the old one.

items.name: Saga Pattern
items.description: Establishes the saga pattern as the standard for managing distributed transactions that span multiple services, coordinating multi-step business processes such as policy issuance or claim settlement through either choreography, where services react to each other's events, or orchestration, where a workflow engine directs the steps and their compensating actions when a stage fails.

items.name: Separate Read and Write Models for High-Scale Scenarios
items.description: Where read and write loads diverge significantly, such as claims status inquiry traffic dwarfing claim updates, or agent portfolio dashboards querying policy data at high volume, systems may maintain distinct write and read models with the read side built as optimized projections. CQRS is reserved for these demonstrated scale cases, not applied by default, because it adds synchronization and consistency complexity.

items.name: Services Under 500 Lines of Business Logic
items.description: A microservice should contain fewer than roughly 500 lines of core business logic, serving as a guardrail for scope rather than a precise quota. A service trending well beyond this size signals that it is absorbing multiple responsibilities, such as combining rating and document generation, and should be evaluated for decomposition.

items.name: Sidecar/Service Mesh
items.description: Mandates a service mesh, Istio or Linkerd, for workloads running in Kubernetes, so cross-cutting concerns including mutual TLS between services, retry and timeout policies, and traffic observability are handled uniformly by the platform's sidecar proxies rather than re-implemented inconsistently inside each insurance application service.

items.name: Single Bounded Context
items.description: Each service lives entirely within one bounded context and never straddles domain boundaries. A service may implement part of the claims context, but it must not blend claims and billing concepts in one codebase or database, keeping the domain model coherent and changes localized.

items.name: Strategic DDD for Domain Modeling
items.description: Strategic domain-driven design techniques, including context mapping and subdomain classification, are used to partition the enterprise into core, supporting, and generic domains such as underwriting, claims, billing, and distribution. This strategic view guides where to invest in custom differentiating capability versus adopting commodity solutions.

items.name: Team Ownership
items.description: Each service has exactly one owning team accountable for its full lifecycle, including build, run, on-call, and eventual decommissioning. Shared or orphaned services are not permitted; if no team can own a proposed service, it should not be created as a separate deployable.

items.name: Ubiquitous Language Enforced
items.description: Within each bounded context, the same business vocabulary is used in conversation, documentation, APIs, and code, with terms defined in the context's glossary. Concepts like insured, member, claimant, and beneficiary must mean exactly one thing inside a context, eliminating the translation errors that arise when engineers and underwriting or claims staff use words differently.

items.name: All Capabilities Exposed via Well-Defined APIs
items.description: Every business capability, whether rating, eligibility, claims intake, or document retrieval, is delivered behind a versioned, documented API designed before implementation begins. No capability may be reachable only through a user interface or a private database connection, so future channels and automation can consume it without rework.

items.name: Business-Aligned Technology
items.description: Requires that every technology decision, from platform selection to integration design, be traceable to the business capabilities and outcomes it supports, so architecture investment across the P&C, Life & Retirement, and group benefits portfolios is justified by demonstrable value such as faster product launch, improved claims experience, or reduced operating cost rather than technical preference.

items.name: Custom Build as Last Resort
items.description: Bespoke development is undertaken only when reuse and commercial options have been formally assessed and found inadequate, typically for capabilities that differentiate the carrier, such as proprietary underwriting models or distinctive customer experiences. A decision to build is documented with the comparative analysis and carries an acknowledged commitment to fund the asset's ongoing maintenance.

items.name: Data as an Asset
items.description: Declares enterprise data, including policy, claims, customer, and financial information, a strategic asset that must have a named owner and steward, defined quality and governance controls, and managed availability for analytics and operations, rather than being treated as an incidental byproduct of the applications that happen to capture it.

items.name: Design for Failure
items.description: Requires every system to assume that dependencies will fail and to degrade gracefully when they do, applying retry with backoff, circuit breakers, and defined fallback behavior so that an outage in one component, such as a third-party data provider or a downstream core system, does not cascade into the loss of quoting, claims intake, or policyholder service.

items.name: Design for Replaceability
items.description: Components are built so they can be swapped out behind stable interfaces, with vendor-specific and infrastructure concerns isolated at the edges of the system. This keeps the enterprise free to replace a rating engine, document platform, or vendor service when the business case changes, without rewriting the consumers around it.

items.name: Evaluate Commercial Solutions
items.description: If no internal capability fits, commercially available software and SaaS offerings are evaluated next against functional fit, total cost of ownership, security and regulatory compliance, and integration with the enterprise architecture. The insurance software market covers most commodity needs, so the burden of proof rests on showing that available products genuinely fall short.

items.name: Internal Services Are First-Class API Consumers
items.description: Internal systems integrate through the same published APIs offered to external consumers, with no privileged back doors into databases or undocumented endpoints. Treating internal consumers identically keeps contracts honest, exercises the APIs at real volume, and guarantees that what partners receive is the same hardened interface the enterprise itself depends on.

items.name: Leverage Existing Capabilities First
items.description: Before any acquisition or build, teams must search the enterprise's existing application, API, and platform inventory for a capability that already meets the need, possibly with configuration or modest extension. Duplicating a function that exists elsewhere in the carrier, such as a second document-generation or address-validation service, requires explicit justification at architecture review.

items.name: Minimize Dependencies Between Systems
items.description: Designs must keep the number and depth of inter-system dependencies as low as practical, interacting through published contracts rather than shared databases or internal implementation details. Each proposed dependency is justified during design review, since every coupling point becomes a constraint on future change to core insurance platforms.

items.name: Use Event-Driven Patterns
items.description: Where systems need awareness of each other's state changes, asynchronous events are preferred over synchronous request chains. Publishing events such as PolicyIssued or ClaimClosed lets consumers subscribe without the producer knowing they exist, removing temporal coupling and protecting upstream systems from downstream outages.

items.name: Auto-Scaling Configured
items.description: Production services must be configured with auto-scaling policies that absorb predictable peaks, such as open enrollment, renewal cycles, and catastrophe-driven claims surges, without manual intervention. Scaling thresholds and limits are documented and tuned based on observed load.

items.name: Documented DR Strategy (Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Active-Active)
items.description: Each production application must declare and document one of the approved recovery patterns: Pilot Light, Warm Standby, or Active-Active, matched to its business criticality tier. The selected pattern, failover procedure, and dependencies are recorded in the architecture repository and approved at solution design review.

items.name: Drift Detection Enabled
items.description: Automated drift detection runs against all managed environments to surface divergence between deployed resources and their declared definitions. Detected drift is triaged, and unauthorized changes are either reverted or formally incorporated into code with review.

items.name: GitOps Workflow
items.description: All infrastructure changes flow through version-controlled repositories with peer-reviewed pull requests and pipeline-driven deployment. The Git history serves as the change record for audit and incident forensics, and only the pipeline identity holds write access to managed environments.

items.name: Hub-Spoke Topology
items.description: Cloud networks follow a hub-spoke design in which shared services, inspection, and hybrid connectivity reside in central hubs and application workloads occupy isolated spokes. Spoke-to-spoke traffic transits the hub so it can be inspected and controlled.

items.name: Identity Integration
items.description: Every landing zone is integrated with the enterprise identity provider at provisioning time, with role-based access granted through standard groups and privileged access managed via just-in-time elevation. Local or standalone identity stores are not permitted.

items.name: Monthly Rightsizing Reviews
items.description: Architecture and platform teams review utilization telemetry each month to identify over-provisioned compute, storage, and database tiers. Recommendations are tracked to closure, and persistent low-utilization resources must be downsized, rescheduled, or decommissioned with the application owner's sign-off.

items.name: Multi-AZ Deployment Required for Production
items.description: All production workloads must be deployed across multiple availability zones so that the loss of a single zone does not interrupt service. Single-zone production deployments require a formal exception with a documented risk acceptance from the application owner.

items.name: NSG/Firewall Rules Documented
items.description: All network security group and firewall rules must be documented with their business justification, owner, and review date, and managed as code where supported. Periodic recertification removes stale rules so the effective network policy stays aligned with what is recorded.

items.name: Network Topology
items.description: Landing zones connect to the enterprise network through the standard topology, including approved address space allocation, routing to shared connectivity hubs, and DNS integration. Workload teams consume the pre-built network rather than designing their own connectivity.

items.name: No Manual Changes
items.description: Direct changes to cloud resources through portals or CLIs are prohibited in managed environments. Any emergency manual intervention must be back-ported into the code base immediately so the declared state remains the single source of truth.

items.name: No Public IPs Except Load Balancers
items.description: Direct public IP assignment to compute resources is prohibited; internet-facing traffic enters only through approved load balancers and application gateways with web application firewall protection. Any other public exposure requires a security-approved exception.

items.name: Policy Guardrails
items.description: Preventive and audit policies are applied to all landing zones at creation, enforcing baseline controls such as allowed regions, encryption requirements, and prohibited services. Guardrails are managed centrally so workload teams operate within compliant boundaries by default.

items.name: Private Endpoints
items.description: Platform services such as databases, storage, and messaging must be consumed over private endpoints within the virtual network rather than public service endpoints. This keeps policyholder and claims data off the public internet path even when the service itself is cloud-managed.

items.name: Quarterly DR Testing
items.description: Disaster recovery plans are exercised at least once per quarter, with failover and failback executed against the documented procedure. Test results, gaps, and remediation actions are recorded, and material failures are escalated to the Architecture Review Board and business continuity management.

items.name: RPO/RTO Documented
items.description: Each system records its recovery point objective and recovery time objective, agreed with the owning business area and aligned to its criticality classification. These targets drive the choice of replication, backup, and failover design, and are validated during DR tests.

items.name: Required Tags: Owner, CostCenter, Environment
